units.title: How .NET code runs
units.blurb: A program's journey from C# source to CPU instructions: the compiler, CIL, metadata, JIT, AOT and the CLR itself.

lessons.title: How a computer understands code
lessons.sub: The CPU, the compiler and the .NET trick

cards.title: The CPU only understands machine code
cards.body:
The CPU is the computer's "brain". It can only do very simple things: add two numbers, compare them, jump to another instruction. These instructions are stored as numbers. That is machine code.

Writing in numbers is painful for people, so we write in programming languages such as C#:
cards.code: Console.WriteLine(40 + 2);
cards.deep: A CPU's instruction set is called its ISA. x64 and ARM64 have different ones: the same operation is encoded with different bytes. That is why a native binary is always built for a specific architecture and OS.

cards.title: A compiler is a translator
cards.body: A program that turns source code into instructions for the machine is called a compiler.

cards.q: What can the CPU run directly?
options: Machine code
C# source
Any programming language
Only what was typed in Notepad
cards.explain: The CPU only understands its own machine code. Everything else has to be translated first.

wrong.1: C# is text for people. The CPU can't read it, so it needs a translation.
wrong.2: The CPU reads no programming language at all, only machine code.

cards.title: The catch: CPUs differ
cards.body:
Most Windows laptops have an x64 CPU. M-series MacBooks and phones use ARM. These are different "machine languages".

A program translated for x64 won't run on ARM. It's like a manual in Japanese handed to someone who only reads English.

cards.q: A game was compiled to x64 machine code and launched on a phone with an ARM CPU. What happens?
options: It won't start
It starts, but runs slower
It translates itself to ARM
It runs as usual
cards.explain: x64 machine code is made of instructions an ARM CPU simply doesn't know.

wrong.2: Machine code doesn't translate itself. That takes special programs called emulators.

cards.title: The .NET trick: translate in two steps
cards.body:
First the compiler turns C# not into machine code but into an intermediate language called CIL. It is the same for every CPU.

Then, on the actual computer and at startup, CIL is translated into machine code for that exact CPU.

Think of sheet music: the composer writes it once, and it can be played on any instrument.
cards.deep: Java works in a similar way with JVM bytecode. The difference is that the CLR was designed from day one for many languages (C#, F#, VB.NET) with a shared type system, the CTS.

cards.title: Managed code: code with a supervisor
cards.body:
A program that runs inside .NET is called managed. It is launched and looked after by the CLR, the Common Language Runtime: it translates CIL into machine code, manages memory and catches errors.

Code that is compiled straight to machine code and runs on its own is called native.

cards.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Intermediate language shared by all CPUs

cards.q: Put the path of a .NET program in order
items: We write C# code
The compiler translates it to CIL
At startup, CIL is translated to machine code
The CPU runs the machine code
cards.explain: These are the four steps from the Microsoft article: compiler, CIL, machine code, execution.

cards.q: Hello.dll was built on an x64 laptop and copied to an ARM Mac that has .NET installed. What happens?
options: It runs
It won't run
It runs only after a rebuild on the Mac
cards.explain: Hello.dll contains CIL, not machine code. The ARM machine code is produced right at startup.

wrong.1: That would be true for a native program. But the .dll holds CIL, which works on any CPU.

lessons.title: Many languages, one .NET
lessons.sub: Compilers, CIL and the shared CLS vocabulary

cards.title: You can write for .NET in many languages
cards.body:
C#, F#, Visual Basic and others. Each has its own compiler, but they all produce the same thing: CIL and metadata, a description of the classes and methods.

That is why a library written in F# can be called from a C# program without any fuss.

cards.title: One method, three languages
cards.body: They look different, but C# and F# produce the same CIL: ldarg.0, ldarg.1, add, ret. We'll see what those lines mean in the next lesson.

cards.q: Who decides how code is written: where semicolons go, how a method is declared?
options: The language compiler
The CLR
The CPU
The operating system
cards.explain: Syntax is the compiler's business. The CLR only sees CIL and has no idea which language you wrote in.

wrong.1: The CLR receives finished CIL. There are no semicolons in it.

cards.title: Same "+", different meaning
cards.body:
Visual Basic checks for overflow by default: its + becomes the CIL instruction add.ovf, an add with a check. If the result doesn't fit in an int, you get an OverflowException.

C# doesn't check by default: the number silently wraps around. The compiler decided what plus means, not the CLR.
cards.code:
int x = int.MaxValue;   // 2,147,483,647
Console.WriteLine(x + 1);
cards.deep: In C# you turn the check on with the checked keyword or the <CheckForOverflowUnderflow> project property. In VB you turn it off with the "Remove integer overflow checks" option. C# rejects a constant expression like int.MaxValue + 1 at compile time (CS0220), which is why the example uses a variable.

cards.q: What does this C# code print with default settings?
cards.code:
int x = int.MaxValue;
Console.WriteLine(x + 1);
options: An OverflowException
cards.explain: Without checked, C# doesn't check for overflow: the top bit flips and you get the smallest int.

wrong.1: That number doesn't fit in an int. The maximum is 2,147,483,647.
wrong.2: That's what Visual Basic would do. C# doesn't check by default.

cards.title: The CLS: a shared vocabulary for languages
cards.body:
Languages have different features. C# has unsigned numbers like uint, but some .NET languages don't.

So that any language can use a library, there is the CLS, the Common Language Specification: rules for what you may expose publicly. The [CLSCompliant(true)] attribute asks the compiler to check those rules.

cards.q: The assembly is marked [assembly: CLSCompliant(true)]. Which line gets a compiler warning?
cards.explain: uint is not part of the CLS, and Count is a public property. The private field _hidden is fine: the CLS only covers what is visible outside the assembly.

cards.q: A public class has methods Run() and run(). Why is that bad from the CLS point of view?
options: Visual Basic is case-insensitive and can't tell which one to call
Similar names slow the program down
The CLR forbids such names
It isn't bad at all
cards.explain: Names that differ only in case break the CLS: for case-insensitive languages they are the same name.

wrong.2: The CLR doesn't mind. This is a rule for language interop, not a runtime restriction.

cards.q: Match each language to its compiler
pairs: Runs the output of any of them

lessons.title: CIL: a stack machine language
lessons.sub: Run CIL with your own hands

cards.title: CIL: instructions for an imaginary machine
cards.body:
CIL (Common Intermediate Language) is a set of simple instructions. They work with a stack, a pile of numbers.

Picture a stack of plates: an instruction puts a number on top or takes the top one off. You can only take from the top.
cards.deep: The stack model keeps compilers and code verification simple: nobody has to allocate registers. The JIT does that later for the specific CPU. x64 has 16 general-purpose registers, ARM64 has 31.

cards.title: The Add method in CIL
cards.body: Here is what the compiler turns a + b into. Comments follow //.
cards.code:
ldarg.0   // push argument a
ldarg.1   // push argument b
add       // pop two numbers, push their sum
ret       // return whatever is on top

cards.task: Press "Step" until the method returns a result. Watch the stack.

cards.q: a = 40, b = 2. What is on top of the stack right after ldarg.1?
cards.code:
ldarg.0
ldarg.1
add
ret
options: Nothing
cards.explain: ldarg.1 pushed b = 2 on top of 40. The addition only happens at the next instruction.

wrong.1: 40 is underneath: ldarg.0 pushed it, then 2 went on top.
wrong.2: 42 only appears after add, and that hasn't run yet.

cards.q: Build the CIL for return a * b + c;
cards.code:
ldarg.0
___
mul
___
add
ret
cards.explain: Push a and b, mul gives a·b, push c, add sums them. The instruction order follows the order of evaluation.

cards.task: Let's test your solution on the machine: a = 5, b = 8, c = 2.

cards.q: Which instructions does CIL have? Select all that apply.
options: Load and store a value
Call a method
Add and multiply
Throw an exception
Draw a window
Connect to Wi-Fi
cards.explain: CIL has loads and stores, calls, arithmetic, branches and exceptions. Windows and networking are libraries that are themselves built from such instructions.

cards.task: Now a broken program. Press "Step" and see what happens.

cards.q: Why did the machine break?
options: add needs two numbers, but the stack has one
The number 40 is too large
A ret is missing
Argument a is wrong
cards.explain: This CIL is invalid: the stack runs dry (stack underflow). In the safety lesson we'll see who catches errors like this.

cards.q: CIL doesn't depend on the CPU. What does that give us?
options: The same CIL becomes machine code for any supported CPU
CIL runs faster than machine code
CIL doesn't need to be compiled
CIL can run without .NET
cards.explain: .NET has a JIT compiler for each CPU, while the CIL is shared by all of them.

wrong.1: The opposite: the CPU doesn't understand CIL, so it still has to be translated to machine code.

lessons.title: What's inside a .dll
lessons.sub: Metadata: a program that describes itself

cards.title: An assembly is a .dll or .exe
cards.body:
The output of compilation is called an assembly. It has two main layers:

CIL: what to do.
Metadata: what the program contains: which classes, and what methods and parameters they have.

cards.title: Metadata is a packing list
cards.body: Like the packing list in a moving box. It lists both what's yours ("class Program, method Add") and what's borrowed, things the program takes from outside ("method WriteLine from the System.Console assembly").
cards.code:
TypeDef     Program
MethodDef   Add(int32, int32) : int32
MethodDef   Main() : void
MemberRef   System.Console::WriteLine(int32)
AssemblyRef System.Console
cards.deep: These are the real metadata table names from the ECMA-335 standard. You can browse them in ildasm or ILSpy, or read them from code with System.Reflection.Metadata.

cards.q: Match each metadata table to what it holds
pairs: This assembly's methods and their parameters
Other code's methods that we call

cards.q: What does metadata describe? Select all that apply.
options: Which classes the assembly has
Method parameters and types
External methods the code calls
Variable values at run time
The user's password
cards.explain: Metadata describes how the program is built. What happens at run time isn't in the file.

cards.title: Code that describes itself
cards.body:
Since the packing list lives right in the file, you don't need separate description files. Older technologies like COM used IDL and type libraries for that.

Metadata powers IDE hints, the debugger and reflection, a program's way of looking at itself:

cards.q: How does the IDE know which methods a class in someone else's .dll has when there is no source?
options: From the metadata inside the .dll
It guesses from the file name
It downloads the source from the internet
It doesn't know
cards.explain: The list of types and method signatures is in the metadata. The IDE simply reads it.

cards.q: Find the line that says "we call someone else's method"
cards.code:
TypeDef     Program
MethodDef   Add(int32, int32) : int32
MethodDef   Main() : void
MemberRef   System.Console::WriteLine(int32)
AssemblyRef System.Console
cards.explain: MemberRef is a reference to a member of another type: here, Console.WriteLine from the System.Console assembly.

cards.title: The file format is PE
cards.body: An assembly is stored in the PE (Portable Executable) format, the same one regular Windows programs use. .NET extended it with a CLR header, metadata and CIL. That's how the system tells a .NET program from a regular one.

cards.q: Hello.dll was built on Windows and runs on Linux. Is it still a PE file?
options: Yes, the assembly format is the same on every OS
No, .NET repackages it into a Linux format
No, on Linux assemblies are .so files
cards.explain: .NET assemblies are PE files on any OS. They are read by the CLR, not by the Linux loader.

wrong.2: .so files are native Linux libraries. A .NET assembly stays a .dll with CIL inside.

lessons.title: JIT: translating at the last moment
lessons.sub: Stubs, the first call and hot methods

cards.title: The JIT translates on the fly
cards.body:
The JIT (just-in-time compiler) is the part of the CLR that turns CIL into machine code while the program is running.

And not the whole program at once, but method by method, when each method is first needed.

cards.title: How it works: stubs
cards.body:
When the CLR loads a class, each method gets a stub in place of machine code.

The first call lands in the stub, and the stub calls the JIT. The JIT compiles the method and points the stub straight at the finished code. Later calls go directly to machine code.

cards.task: Call Add twice. How many times does the JIT kick in?

cards.q: A program calls Add 1,000 times. How many times does the JIT compile Add?
cards.explain: Once, on the first call. After that the stub leads straight to finished machine code. (There's a twist for modern .NET at the end of the lesson.)

wrong.1: Compiling every time would be very slow. That's exactly what the stub is for.

cards.q: Main calls Add and Log. Nobody calls Unused. How many methods does the JIT compile if you run Main?
cards.explain: Main, Add and Log. Unused stays a stub: the JIT doesn't waste time on code nobody needs.

wrong.1: Nobody calls Unused, so the JIT never gets to it.

cards.task: Check it: press "Call" on Main once.

cards.q: The program was closed and started again. Can it reuse the machine code the JIT produced last time?
options: No: it lived in the process memory and died with the process
Yes, the JIT saves it to disk
Only the code for Main
cards.explain: JIT output belongs to one process. A new run means a new compilation. The next lesson shows how to avoid that.

cards.q: What is true about the JIT? Select all that apply.
options: It compiles only what gets called
It knows the exact CPU it is running on
The first call of a method is slower than later ones
Its code is shared by all running copies of the program
It compiles the whole program at install time
cards.explain: The JIT saves work and tunes code for the CPU, but pays with a slower first call, and its code isn't shared between processes.

cards.title: The modern JIT works in two passes
cards.body:
.NET Core 3.0 and later turn on tiered compilation.

First a method is compiled quickly with no optimizations: Tier 0. If it gets called often (the threshold is about 30 calls), the JIT recompiles it in the background, this time optimized: Tier 1. The program starts fast and still runs fast.
cards.deep: Long-running loops get OSR (on-stack replacement, .NET 7+): the loop switches to optimized code mid-execution. Dynamic PGO (on by default since .NET 8) gathers statistics at Tier 0 and uses them when building Tier 1. Methods from ReadyToRun images also count as an "initial tier" and get recompiled to Tier 1 once they warm up.

cards.task: Tiered mode is on. Keep calling Add (the "×10" button speeds things up) until it reaches Tier 1.

cards.q: With tiered JIT, how many times is Add compiled over 1,000 calls?
cards.explain: Twice: a quick Tier 0 on the first call, and an optimized Tier 1 once the method got hot.

lessons.title: Compiling ahead of time
lessons.sub: NGen, ReadyToRun and Native AOT

cards.title: The JIT has a cost
cards.body:
On every launch the program spends time turning CIL into machine code. Usually you don't notice, but for large apps and cloud services that restart often, startup time matters.

The fix is to compile in advance: AOT (ahead-of-time).

cards.title: NGen: the approach from the Microsoft article
cards.body:
Classic .NET Framework had NGen.exe for this. It differs from the JIT in three ways:

1. It compiles before launch, not during.
2. It compiles the whole assembly at once, not one method at a time.
3. It saves the code to disk, in the Native Image Cache, and different processes can share it.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Compiles a method on its first call
Compiles the whole assembly in advance
Hands the first call to the JIT

cards.title: And in modern .NET
cards.body:
NGen exists only in .NET Framework. .NET 5 and later offer two options:

ReadyToRun: the file contains precompiled machine code plus CIL, just in case. Startup is faster, and the JIT can later reoptimize hot methods. Property: <PublishReadyToRun>.

Native AOT: the whole program becomes a single native file. There is no JIT in it at all, and you don't need .NET installed. Property: <PublishAot>.
cards.deep: Native AOT requires trimming: the compiler throws away everything it can't reach statically. Hence the limits: no Assembly.LoadFrom or Reflection.Emit, and reflection over types never mentioned in code may fail to find them. Analyzers flag the risky spots with IL2xxx and IL3xxx warnings.

cards.task: Press "Start" and see who prints 42 first.

cards.q: Why is a ReadyToRun file bigger than a regular one?
options: It holds both precompiled machine code and CIL
All of .NET is built into it
It isn't compressed
It stores the source code
cards.explain: The CIL is kept so the JIT can recompile code if the precompiled version doesn't fit or the method gets hot.

wrong.1: Native AOT carries the whole runtime inside. ReadyToRun still relies on the installed .NET.

cards.q: An app loads plugins from a folder at run time (Assembly.LoadFrom) and generates code (Reflection.Emit). Will Native AOT work?
options: No: Native AOT can't load or create code at run time
Yes, with no limits
Yes, if you turn on ReadyToRun
cards.explain: Native AOT has no JIT, so there is nothing to compile new code at run time.

cards.q: You want faster startup but don't want to change your code. What do you turn on?
options: ReadyToRun
Native AOT
NGen
Disable the JIT
cards.explain: ReadyToRun is compatible with everything: if the precompiled code isn't enough, the regular JIT steps in.

wrong.1: Native AOT may need code changes: reflection and dynamic loading are limited.
wrong.2: NGen only works in .NET Framework.

cards.q: Turn on Native AOT in the project file
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <___>true</___>
</PropertyGroup>
cards.explain: Set PublishAot=true, and dotnet publish builds a native file for the target platform.

cards.q: Which is which
pairs: Precompiled code and CIL in one file

lessons.title: Type safety
lessons.sub: Verification: then and now

cards.title: What type safety means
cards.body:
A type says what's stored in memory: a number, a string, an array. Type-safe code touches memory only in ways the type allows: it doesn't read a string as a number or step past the end of an array.

That protects objects from each other, against both honest mistakes and attacks.

cards.title: Three promises
cards.body:
According to the Microsoft article, the CLR relies on three rules for type-safe code:

1. A reference to a type is always compatible with that type.
2. Only the operations defined for an object are invoked on it.
3. An object is what it claims to be.

cards.q: Which rule is broken?
pairs: Reference is compatible with its type
A string is read as an array of numbers
A number gets a method call it doesn't have
An object is what it claims to be
An object poses as a different type

cards.q: What happens?
cards.code:
object o = "hello";
int[] a = (int[])o;
options: InvalidCastException: the CLR won't let a string pass as an array
a ends up holding the character codes
The code won't compile
Nothing
cards.explain: The compiler lets it through: an object could be anything. But at run time the CLR checks the real type and throws.

wrong.2: It compiles: casting object to int[] is legal until it turns out there's a string inside.

cards.q: What happens?
cards.code:
int[] a = new int[3];
a[5] = 1;
options: IndexOutOfRangeException
It writes 1 into the memory past the array
The array grows to 6 elements
Nothing
cards.explain: The CLR checks array bounds on every access. Safe code can't write past the end.

wrong.1: That could happen in C or C++. In managed code the CLR won't let you cross the bound.

cards.title: Verification in .NET Framework
cards.body:
Before JIT compilation, CIL went through verification: can we prove the code is type-safe? If security policy required verified code and the check failed, you got an exception at startup.

The verifier plays it safe: it also rejects some code that is safe. For example, any code with pointers (unsafe).

cards.q: Which line would the verifier reject?
cards.explain: A pointer means unsafe code. Here it's actually harmless (the address of a local variable), but the verifier can't prove that, so it rejects any code with pointers.

cards.q: What does verification check? Select all that apply.
options: Memory is accessed through the correct types
The CIL is well-formed, e.g. the stack has enough numbers
The algorithm works correctly
There are no memory leaks
cards.explain: Verification is about memory safety and well-formed CIL. It doesn't check program logic.

cards.title: And today?
cards.body:
.NET Core and .NET 5+ dropped the old security policy system (CAS), and the CLR does not verify CIL at startup.

Type safety now rests on the compiler and run-time checks: array bounds and type casts, exactly what you just saw. You can check CIL by hand with the ILVerify tool.
cards.deep: That's why unsafe code in modern .NET simply runs if the project allows it (<AllowUnsafeBlocks>). The responsibility is on the programmer. Untrusted code is now isolated with processes and containers, not inside the CLR.

cards.q: Remember the broken CIL from lesson 3 (add with only one number on the stack)? What would the .NET Framework verifier do with it?
options: Reject it: that CIL is invalid
Let it through
Fix the bug itself
cards.explain: Checking that CIL is well-formed is exactly the verifier's job: badly generated CIL breaks the safety guarantees.

lessons.title: Startup and CLR services
lessons.sub: Who launches the program and what the CLR gives it

cards.title: The CLR is more than the JIT
cards.body:
While a program runs, the CLR provides services:

Garbage collection: frees memory that is no longer needed.
Safety: type and bounds checks.
Native interop: calling C and C++ libraries.
Cross-language debugging.
Deployment and versioning of libraries.

cards.q: Which CLR service helps?
pairs: Call a function from a C library
A breakpoint in an F# library called from C#
Two programs need different library versions

cards.title: How Windows launched a .NET program
cards.body:
Here's how the Microsoft article describes it for .NET Framework:

The Windows loader sees a "this is a managed module" flag in the file header and loads mscoree.dll. The _CorValidateImage function checks that the file holds valid managed code and replaces the entry point with the CLR's entry point.
cards.deep: On 64-bit Windows, _CorValidateImage also converts the in-memory image from PE32 to PE32+. Its counterpart, _CorImageUnloading, tells the loader when the image is unloaded.

cards.q: Put the .NET Framework startup in order
items: Double-click hello.exe
Windows sees the "managed module" flag
mscoree.dll is loaded
_CorValidateImage checks the code and swaps the entry point
The CLR runs Main
cards.explain: First the OS, then mscoree.dll, an image check, and control passes to the CLR.

cards.title: And in modern .NET
cards.body: The chain is the same on Windows, Linux and macOS. It starts with a tiny launcher, hello.exe (the apphost), or the command dotnet hello.dll.
cards.deep: hostfxr reads hello.runtimeconfig.json and picks a suitable installed runtime using roll-forward rules. hostpolicy reads hello.deps.json and builds the list of assemblies to load. Native AOT skips this chain: the file is native from the start.

cards.q: Assemble the modern startup chain
items: dotnet hello.dll
hostfxr picks the .NET version
hostpolicy finds dependencies
coreclr starts the CLR
Main() is called
cards.explain: Host, version choice, dependencies, CLR, your code.

cards.q: The computer has no .NET. Someone runs hello.exe, a regular build, not Native AOT. What do they see?
options: A message saying .NET must be installed to run it
The program starts
Windows embeds the CLR into the file
A blue screen
cards.explain: hostfxr found no suitable runtime. The launcher shows "You must install or update .NET to run this application" with a download link.

wrong.1: Without .NET installed, only Native AOT or a self-contained build, which carries the runtime with it, will start.

cards.q: Main calls Add for the first time. What happens?
options: Stub, then JIT, then machine code, then execution
The CPU runs the CIL directly
The CLR reads and interprets the C# source
Add was already compiled at install time
cards.explain: Each method is compiled on its first call and then executed. That goes on until the program ends.

cards.title: The whole journey
cards.body: This is managed execution. You've walked through every step. All that's left is the final challenge.

lessons.title: Final: the journey of a byte
lessons.sub: Everything mixed: test yourself

cards.q: The full path of a .NET program
items: C# code
Compiler
CIL and metadata in a .dll
The host starts the CLR
JIT on first call
Machine code runs
cards.explain: Managed execution from start to finish.

cards.q: Build the CIL for return (a + b) * c;
cards.code:
ldarg.0
ldarg.1
___
ldarg.2
___
ret
cards.explain: Parentheses first: a + b means add. Then push c and multiply with mul.

cards.q: Hello.dll and a Native AOT build of hello were copied to a computer without .NET. What runs?
options: Only the Native AOT build
Both
Only Hello.dll
Neither
cards.explain: Native AOT is a standalone native file. Hello.dll needs the CLR, and there isn't one.

cards.q: Where is the method declared in this same assembly described?
cards.code:
AssemblyRef System.Console
MemberRef   System.Console::WriteLine(int32)
TypeDef     Program
MethodDef   Add(int32, int32) : int32
cards.explain: MethodDef is for your own methods. MemberRef is for references to other code's.

cards.q: How many times does the JIT compile a method that was never called?
cards.explain: The JIT only works on demand. A method nobody calls stays a stub.

cards.q: What's inside a regular .NET assembly? Select all that apply.
options: CIL
Metadata
A PE header
Machine code for every CPU at once
The C# source code
cards.explain: A regular assembly has no machine code: the JIT will produce it. No source code either.

cards.q: A public method in a C# library takes a uint. Someone wants to call it from a language without unsigned numbers. What would have warned you in advance?
options: [assembly: CLSCompliant(true)]: the compiler would issue a warning
The JIT on the first call
The garbage collector
Nothing, the CLR converts it on its own
cards.explain: The CLS is a set of rules for public APIs, and CLSCompliant turns on the check.

cards.q: What exists only in .NET Framework?
options: NGen
ReadyToRun
Native AOT
JIT
cards.explain: .NET 5+ uses ReadyToRun and Native AOT instead of NGen.

cards.q: What happens?
cards.code:
object o = 42;
string s = (string)o;
options: InvalidCastException
s becomes "42"
The code won't compile
s becomes null
cards.explain: A cast is not a conversion. The CLR sees that o holds a number, not a string, and throws. o.ToString() would give you a string.

wrong.1: That takes o.ToString(). A (string) cast only checks the type.

cards.q: Who does this?
Why does the same Hello.dll run on both x64 and ARM64?
options: It contains CIL, and there's a JIT for each CPU
It contains machine code for both
ARM64 can run x64 code
It doesn't
cards.explain: The big idea from lesson 1: CIL is shared, machine code is produced on the spot.

cards.q: Tiered JIT is on. A method has been called 5 times. What state is it in?
options: Tier 0: it's nowhere near the "hot" threshold yet
Tier 1
Still a stub
Native AOT
cards.explain: Tier 0 appeared on the first call. Tier 1 comes after about 30 calls.

units.title: Types and memory
units.blurb: Value and reference types, the stack and the heap, boxing, argument passing and what makes string special, on a rig that shows every variable and every object.

lessons.title: Value types and reference types
lessons.sub: Why the same line behaves differently

cards.title: Two kinds of types
cards.body:
Every type in C# is one of two kinds.

Value types: int, double, bool, any struct. The variable holds the value itself.

Reference types: any class, string, arrays. The variable holds only the object's address, a reference. The object itself lives elsewhere, on the heap.

A value type is like a note with a number on it: you hand over a copy and keep your own. A reference type is like a house address: give it to a friend, and you both walk into the same house.

cards.task: Step through the program twice: once with Point as a struct and once as a class. Watch the stack and the heap.

steps.note: p1 is a struct: both fields live right in the variable, on the stack.
p2 = p1 copies the whole struct. Now there are two independent points.
We change p2. p1 is not affected.
Prints 1: p1 has its own copy.
A Point object is created on the heap. p1 holds only a reference to it.
p2 = p1 copies the reference. Both variables lead to the same object.
We change the object through p2. It's the same object p1 points to.
Prints 100: p1 and p2 are the same object.

cards.q: Point is a struct. What does the code print?
options: A compile error
cards.explain: Assigning a struct copies all of it. p2 is a separate copy, and changes to it don't show up in p1.

cards.q: And if Point is a class?
options: NullReferenceException
cards.explain: For a class, only the reference is copied. p1 and p2 lead to one object, so a change made through p2 is visible through p1.

cards.q: Which of these are value types? Select all that apply.
options: int
bool
DateTime
string
int[]
List<int>
cards.explain: DateTime is a struct. string and arrays are reference types, even if they hold nothing but numbers.

cards.title: How to tell which is which
cards.body:
struct and enum are value types. class, interface, delegates, arrays and string are reference types.

Can't remember? Hover over the type in your IDE: it will say struct or class.
cards.deep: A record struct is a value type; a plain record (a record class) is a reference type. int? is Nullable<int>, also a struct: the value plus a HasValue flag.

cards.q: Point is a class with no Equals override. What does a.Equals(b) return?
options: False
True
A compile error
cards.explain: These are two different objects on the heap. A class's default Equals compares references. For a struct it would compare fields and return True.

wrong.1: A struct would give True: its default Equals compares fields.

cards.q: When does a struct make sense?
options: A small value that behaves like a number: a coordinate, a color, a date
A big object with a dozen fields that gets passed around a lot
An object that is modified from many places in the program
cards.explain: A struct is copied on every assignment and every call. That's expensive for big data, and changes to a copy don't reach the original.
cards.deep: Microsoft's guideline: a struct should be under 16 bytes, immutable, and logically represent a single value.

cards.q: Point is a class. After which line does a.X become 50?
cards.explain: b is a reference to the same object as a. c is a completely different object, even though it has the same values.

lessons.title: The stack and the heap
lessons.sub: Where variables and objects live

cards.title: The stack: a method's notepad
cards.body:
When a method is called, it gets a slice of memory on the stack called a frame. The frame holds the local variables and parameters.

When the method returns, the whole frame is thrown away. That's very fast: no cleanup needed.

cards.title: The heap: a warehouse for objects
cards.body:
Class instances created with new live on the heap. They aren't tied to a method and live as long as anything still references them.

Unused objects are cleaned up by the garbage collector. That's the next unit.

cards.task: Step through and watch the frame for the Heal method appear and disappear.

steps.note: count is a number and lives right in Main's frame.
A Hero object is created on the heap. Main's frame holds a reference to it.
Calling Heal pushes a new frame onto the stack. h gets a copy of the reference, amount a copy of the number.
h leads to the same object as hero, so we modify it.
Heal returned and its frame is gone. The object on the heap stays: hero still references it.

cards.q: Where does the local variable int count from Main live?
options: In Main's frame on the stack
On the heap
In the assembly metadata
In special memory reserved for numbers
cards.explain: Local variables of value types live in their method's frame.

cards.title: Myth: "structs always live on the stack"
cards.body:
A value type lives wherever it's declared:

a local variable lives in a frame on the stack;
a class field lives inside the object, so on the heap;
an array element lives inside the array, also on the heap.
cards.deep: The JIT may keep a local variable in a CPU register and never touch memory. Recent .NET versions sometimes even put class instances on the stack when the JIT can prove they never leave the method (escape analysis). These are optimizations: they don't change how the code behaves.

cards.task: An array of two points: step through both versions and compare how many objects end up on the heap.

steps.note: The array is an object on the heap. For structs, space for both points is right inside it.
The point is written straight into the array slot. No new objects.
Total on the heap: one object, the array itself.
An array of classes holds only references. For now they are null.
Each point is a separate object on the heap; the array holds a reference to it.
Total: three objects, the array and two points.

cards.q: An array of 1,000 Point structs and an array of 1,000 Point classes, all elements filled. How many objects are on the heap in each case?
cards.explain: An array of structs is one object with the points inside it. An array of classes is the array itself plus 1,000 separate point objects.
cards.deep: That's why arrays of structs are faster to iterate: the data sits contiguously and plays well with the CPU cache. Game engines and ECS rely on this.

cards.q: What lives on the heap? Select all that apply.
options: A class instance created with new
A struct field inside a class instance
The elements of an int[]
A local int variable
A struct parameter of a method
cards.explain: Anything inside an object or array lives with it on the heap. Local variables and parameters live in a stack frame.

cards.q: A method returned. Its local variable referenced an object, and nothing else references it. What happens to the object?
options: It became garbage; the garbage collector will clean it up later
It's deleted immediately along with the frame
It lives until the program ends
cards.explain: The frame disappears right away, but the object on the heap doesn't. It just became unreachable, and the garbage collector will reclaim it.

lessons.title: Boxing
lessons.sub: When a number suddenly ends up on the heap

cards.title: A number in an object variable
cards.body:
object is a reference type. If you put a number into it, .NET creates a "box" on the heap with a copy of the number and stores a reference to it in the variable. That's boxing.

Getting the number back out is unboxing.

cards.task: Step through and see where the box appears.

steps.note: A plain number on the stack.
Boxing: a box with a copy of 42 appeared on the heap, and o holds a reference to it.
We change n. The box doesn't change: it has its own copy.
Unboxing: the copy from the box is back on the stack. m = 42.

cards.q: What is m?
options: An exception is thrown
cards.explain: The box got a copy of 42. Changing n after boxing doesn't touch it.

cards.q: What happens?
cards.code:
object o = 42;
long x = (long)o;
options: InvalidCastException
A compile error
cards.explain: You can only unbox to the exact same type. The box holds an int, not a long. The right way: (long)(int)o.

wrong.1: That would work for a plain int: (long)n. But unboxing requires the exact type.
wrong.2: The compiler allows it: an object could be anything. The error happens at run time.

cards.title: Where boxing hides
cards.body:
A number becomes an object when you put it where an object or an interface is expected:

IComparable c = 5;
old collections like ArrayList;
methods with an object parameter, such as Console.WriteLine("{0}", n).

Every boxing is a new object on the heap and more work for the garbage collector. Generic collections (List<int>) store numbers without boxes.
cards.deep: Boxing in a hot loop is a classic source of extra allocations, and it shows up in a profiler. String interpolation $"{n}" in C# 10+ goes through an interpolation handler with generic methods and usually avoids boxing.

cards.q: Where does boxing happen? Select all that apply.
options: object o = 5;
IComparable c = 5;
arrayList.Add(5);
list.Add(5);  // List<int>
int x = 5 + 5;
cards.explain: object, an interface and ArrayList all expect a reference, so a box is needed. List<int> stores the int as is.

cards.q: Which line creates an object on the heap?
cards.explain: object c = b is boxing: a box appears on the heap. Unboxing on line 4 creates no new objects.

cards.q: Why is List<int> better than ArrayList for numbers?
options: It stores int as is: no boxing and no casts
It's thread-safe
It compresses numbers
cards.explain: ArrayList stores object: every number is boxed on the way in and unboxed on the way out. The generic knows the exact type.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A copy of the value moves to the heap
The copy comes back from the box into a variable

lessons.title: Passing to a method
lessons.sub: Copy, ref, out and in

cards.title: By default, a copy
cards.body:
When you call a method, each argument is copied into its parameter.

For a struct, the whole struct is copied. For a class, only the reference: the method gets the address of the same object.

cards.task: Step through the call to Move in both versions.

steps.note: p is a struct in Main's frame.
Move got a copy of the whole struct.
We change the copy in Move's frame.
Move's frame is gone, and the copy with it.
Prints 1.
p is a reference to an object on the heap.
Move got a copy of the reference, to the same object.
We change the object on the heap, shared by p and q.
Move's frame is gone; the object stays modified.
Prints 99.

cards.q: Point is a struct. What does the program print?
cards.explain: Move changed its own copy. The variable p in Main stayed the same.

cards.title: ref: pass the variable itself
cards.body:
With ref, the method gets not a copy but access to the caller's variable.

out is the same, but the method must assign a value (like in int.TryParse).
in passes by reference, but read-only: a big struct doesn't have to be copied.
cards.code:
static void Move(ref Point q) => q.X = 99;
Move(ref p);
cards.deep: in with a regular (non-readonly) struct can force the compiler to make "defensive copies" when calling its methods, in case a method changes fields. That's why big structs are declared readonly struct.

cards.task: Now Move(ref p). See what q points to.

steps.note: p is a struct in Main's frame.
q is not a copy but a reference to the variable p in Main.
p itself changes, right in Main's frame.
Move returned.
Prints 99.

cards.q: Point is a class, p = (5, 5). What is p.X after Reset(p)?
options: NullReferenceException
cards.explain: The method replaced its own copy of the reference with a new object. The variable p still leads to the old object. To replace p, you need ref.

wrong.1: That would happen with ref Point q. Without ref, the method only changes its own copy of the reference.

cards.task: Check it on the rig: what happens to q inside Reset.

steps.note: The object (5, 5) on the heap.
q is a copy of the reference p.
q now leads to a new object. p still leads to the old one.
Reset's frame is gone. The new object became garbage, and p didn't change.

cards.q: Match each modifier to its meaning
pairs: The method reads and changes the caller's variable
The method must assign a value

cards.q: Why pass a big struct as in?
options: To avoid copying it on every call and to forbid changes
So the method can change it
So it moves to the heap
cards.explain: in passes an address instead of copying every field, and the compiler won't let the method change it.

lessons.title: string: a special type
lessons.sub: A reference type that behaves like a value

cards.title: A string can't be changed
cards.body:
string is a reference type: the text lives on the heap. But a string is immutable. Any "edit" creates a new string, and the old one stays exactly as it was.

That's why strings are safe to pass anywhere: nobody can mess up your text.

cards.task: Step through and see what += does.

steps.note: The string "kit" is on the heap; a holds a reference.
b leads to the same string.
+= doesn't change "kit": a new string "kitten" is created, and b now leads to it.
Prints "kit".

cards.q: What does the code print?
options: kit
kitten
ten
cards.explain: The string "kit" didn't change. b got a reference to a new string; a didn't.

cards.q: Two strings with the same text were built in different ways. What does a == b return?
options: True
False
cards.explain: The == operator on string compares text, not references. These are different objects, but the text is the same.

cards.title: Concatenating strings in a loop is a bad idea
cards.body:
s += x in a loop creates a new string every time and copies all the accumulated text into it. 10,000 iterations means 10,000 garbage strings and work that grows quadratically.

StringBuilder collects text in a mutable buffer and builds the string once at the end.

cards.q: How many new strings does this loop create?
cards.explain: Each += creates a new string. The literal "x" is only one object, though: it's interned.

cards.title: Interning
cards.body:
Identical string literals in a program are one and the same object: the CLR keeps them in the intern pool.

Strings built at run time don't go there unless you call string.Intern.
cards.deep: That's why ReferenceEquals("abc", "abc") is usually true, but false for a string with the same text from a StringBuilder. Comparing strings by reference is a bug: use == or string.Equals with the right StringComparison.

cards.q: What is true about string? Select all that apply.
options: It's a reference type
Once created, a string can't be changed
== compares text
The string's text lives on the stack
s.Replace("a", "b") changes the original string
cards.explain: Replace, ToUpper and other methods return a new string. If you don't keep the result, nothing changes.

cards.q: Build a fast way to join words
cards.explain: StringBuilder.Append writes into the buffer without creating intermediate strings.

lessons.title: Final: where data lives
lessons.sub: Everything about types and memory: test yourself

cards.q: Size is a struct. What is a.W?
cards.explain: A struct is copied whole: b is an independent copy.

cards.q: And if Size is a class?
cards.explain: For a class, the reference is copied: a and b are one object.

cards.q: What ends up on the heap? Select all that apply.
options: new List<int>()
A local int variable
An int field inside a class instance
object o = 3.14;
bool flag = true;
cards.explain: Class instances, everything inside them, and boxes from boxing live on the heap. Local value-type variables live on the stack.

cards.q: Point is a class, p = (5, 5). What happens to p.X after the call?
cards.code:
static void Reset(Point q) => q = new Point(0, 0);
Reset(p);
options: It stays 5
It becomes 0
NullReferenceException
cards.explain: The method replaced its own copy of the reference. Without ref, the variable p doesn't change.

cards.q: What happens?
cards.code:
object o = 1;
double d = (double)o;
options: InvalidCastException
A compile error
cards.explain: The box holds an int. You can only unbox to int and convert afterwards: (double)(int)o.

cards.q: Which line changes nothing?
cards.explain: ToUpper returns a new string, and the result is thrown away. The program prints "hi!".

cards.q: An array of 100 Point class instances, all filled. How many objects are on the heap?
cards.explain: The array itself plus 100 separate points.

cards.q: What is n?
cards.explain: With ref, the method works with the variable n itself.

cards.q: A method returned. What disappeared immediately?
options: Its stack frame with all local variables
All the objects it created
Nothing; the garbage collector cleans up everything
cards.explain: The frame is discarded instantly. Objects on the heap live as long as something references them.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Boxing: a box on the heap

cards.q: Pass a big struct without copying it and without permission to change it
cards.code:
static double Length(___ Vector3 v) =>
    Math.Sqrt(v.X * v.X + v.Y * v.Y + v.Z * v.Z);
cards.explain: in passes by reference, read-only.

units.title: Garbage collection and resources
units.blurb: Roots and reachability, generations and the LOH, finalizers, IDisposable and using, SafeHandle and memory leaks. You run the collections yourself and see who survives.

lessons.title: How the GC finds garbage
lessons.sub: Roots, reachability and cycles

cards.title: Nobody writes delete
cards.body: In C# you create objects with new but never delete them by hand. The garbage collector (GC) does that: every so often it finds objects nobody needs anymore and frees their memory.

cards.title: Roots and reachability
cards.body:
The GC starts from roots: local variables of running methods and static fields. From there it follows references. Everything it can reach is alive. The rest is garbage.

Think of a bunch of balloons: cut the string in your hand, and every balloon tied to it floats away.
cards.deep: CPU registers, GC handles (pinned objects, for example) and the finalization queue also count as roots. The JIT knows where a variable is last used: in a Release build an object can become garbage before the method ends. That's what GC.KeepAlive is for: it extends the lifetime up to a given line.

cards.task: Get rid of Log while keeping Order, Item and Price.

cards.q: order = null. What happens to Order → Item → Price?
options: All three become garbage
Only Order is removed
Nothing: their references to each other keep them alive
cards.explain: Item and Price are reachable only through Order. No path from a root means the whole chain is garbage.

cards.task: A and B reference each other. Clear the root and run a collection. Are they removed?

cards.q: Why doesn't the A ⇄ B cycle bother the collector?
options: The GC looks for what is reachable from roots; it doesn't count references
The GC breaks cycles on a timer
It does bother it: that's a memory leak
cards.explain: Cycles are a problem where memory is freed by reference counting (like ARC in Swift). Tracing from roots simply never reaches them, so they get removed.

cards.title: What the GC does next
cards.body:
After freeing the garbage, the GC slides live objects closer together. That's compaction. New objects are then allocated back to back, very quickly.

Program threads are usually paused briefly during a collection.
cards.deep: Allocation in .NET is just bumping a pointer in the thread's "allocation context", so new is very cheap. What's expensive is surviving collections. There are Workstation and Server GC modes, background Gen 2 collection and GCSettings.LatencyMode.

cards.q: What counts as a GC root? Select all that apply.
options: A local variable of a running method
A static field
A field of an object nobody references
Any object older than a minute
cards.explain: Roots are things that are definitely in use right now: thread stacks and static fields. A field of an unreachable object is not a root.

cards.q: When does a garbage collection run?
options: When the runtime decides, usually when Gen 0 fills up
As soon as an object becomes garbage
Only when GC.Collect() is called
Exactly once per second
cards.explain: Garbage can sit around for a while. The GC kicks in once enough new memory has been allocated. More on that in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Generations
lessons.sub: Gen 0, 1, 2 and the large object heap

cards.title: Most objects die young
cards.body:
Temporary strings, per-request objects, iterators: they live for a fraction of a second. That's why the heap is split into generations:

Gen 0: new objects.
Gen 1: survived one collection.
Gen 2: long-lived objects.

A Gen 0 collection is frequent and fast: it only looks at the young.
cards.deep: So a Gen 0 collection doesn't have to walk the whole heap, the CLR marks spots in older generations that got a reference to a young object in a "card table". A write barrier sets the mark on every assignment to a reference field.

cards.task: The temporary objects Temp1 and Temp2 should go away, while Cache makes it to Gen 2.

cards.q: An object is in Gen 1. A Gen 0 collection runs. What happens to it?
options: Nothing: a Gen 0 collection doesn't even look at it
It's removed
It moves to Gen 2
cards.explain: A collection of generation N covers generations 0 through N. It doesn't touch older ones.

cards.title: The LOH: the large object heap
cards.body:
Objects of 85,000 bytes or more, usually big arrays, go straight to a separate heap, the LOH (large object heap).

It's collected only together with Gen 2 and isn't compacted by default: moving big chunks of memory is expensive.
cards.deep: That's why big temporary arrays are a common cause of full collections and fragmentation. The cure is ArrayPool<T>.Shared: rent a buffer and return it. Since .NET 5 there's also the POH, a heap for pinned objects.

cards.task: Clear both references and get both objects removed. Which collection can handle Buffer?

cards.q: A byte[100_000] became garbage. Who cleans it up?
options: Only a full collection (Gen 2)
The next Gen 0 collection
Nobody: the LOH is never cleaned
cards.explain: 100,000 bytes is above the 85,000 threshold, so the array is on the LOH. And the LOH is collected together with Gen 2.

cards.q: What is true about generations? Select all that apply.
options: New objects go to Gen 0
Survive a collection and you move to the next generation
A Gen 2 collection is the most expensive
Objects in Gen 2 are never removed
Every collection checks every object
cards.explain: Gen 2 objects do get removed, but only by a full collection, which is rare.

cards.q: Why doesn't a huge cache that lives for the whole program slow down frequent collections?
options: It quickly lands in Gen 2, and frequent Gen 0 collections don't walk it
The GC skips objects named Cache
The cache lives on the stack
cards.explain: A long-lived object moves to Gen 2 and from then on costs frequent collections almost nothing.

cards.q: Is calling GC.Collect() "to clean up memory" a good idea?
options: Usually not: a full collection is expensive and also promotes live objects
Yes, it speeds the program up
Yes, it makes the GC do less work
cards.explain: The GC knows when to collect. A forced collection pauses threads and makes live objects "older", which makes them more expensive to clean up later.

lessons.title: Finalizers
lessons.sub: A last resort you can't rely on

cards.title: A finalizer is a last resort
cards.body:
A class can declare a finalizer, ~Name(). The GC calls it before freeing the object's memory.

It was invented for things the GC doesn't know about: file handles, sockets, OS memory.

cards.title: What a finalizer costs
cards.body:
An object with a finalizer can't be removed right away. The GC puts it on the finalization queue, a separate thread calls the finalizer at some later point, and only the next collection frees the memory.

The object lives longer and has time to get promoted to an older generation.

cards.task: Clear both references and make sure F is really removed. Count how many steps it took.

cards.q: How many garbage collections does it take to free the memory of an object with a finalizer?
options: At least two: the first queues it, the second frees it
One
None: the finalizer frees the memory itself
cards.explain: The first collection finds the object and queues it. The finalizer runs. The next collection of its generation frees the memory.

cards.q: When does the finalizer run?
options: Unknown: once the GC finds the object and the finalizer thread gets to it
Right when the method returns
Right after you assign null
cards.explain: The timing isn't guaranteed: maybe in a millisecond, maybe in a minute.

cards.title: What you can't trust a finalizer with
cards.body:
The timing isn't guaranteed.
The order between objects isn't guaranteed: a neighboring object may already be finalized.
In .NET Core and .NET 5+, finalizers aren't run at all when the program exits.

A file that only the finalizer closes may never be fully written.

cards.q: What is true about finalizers? Select all that apply.
options: An object with a finalizer lives longer
The order of calls between objects isn't guaranteed
They run on a separate thread
They run the instant an object becomes garbage
In .NET 8 they're guaranteed to run on program exit
cards.explain: A finalizer is a backup mechanism. For timely cleanup there's Dispose, the next lesson.

cards.q: Which line in this finalizer is dangerous?
cards.explain: _writer is another managed object. By the time ~Logger runs, it may already be finalized and closed. A finalizer should touch only unmanaged resources.

cards.q: A regular class with no native resources. Does it need a finalizer?
options: No: it would only slow collection down
Yes, just in case
Yes, otherwise the memory won't be freed
cards.explain: The GC frees managed memory on its own. An unneeded finalizer means an extra queue and an extra collection.

lessons.title: IDisposable and using
lessons.sub: Release a resource now, not someday

cards.title: Resources the GC doesn't know about
cards.body:
A file, a network connection, a database connection: these are OS resources. The GC only sees memory and has no idea an object is holding a file open.

If you wait for the GC, the file may stay open for who knows how long.

cards.task: Open the file, then "forget" it (= null) and try to open it again. Get the second open to succeed without Dispose.

cards.title: IDisposable: release it now
cards.body:
Classes that hold such resources implement IDisposable: the Dispose() method closes the resource right away.

using calls Dispose() automatically, even if an exception was thrown inside.

cards.task: Now open the file twice the right way: with Dispose() or using.

cards.q: An exception was thrown inside a using block. What happens to the resource?
options: Dispose() is still called
It stays open
The exception is swallowed
cards.explain: using expands into try/finally, and finally runs no matter what.

cards.q: using is syntactic sugar. What does it expand into?
cards.explain: try/finally guarantees Dispose() on both a normal exit and an exception.

cards.title: Your own class with a resource
cards.body: If a class owns an IDisposable field, it must implement IDisposable too and release the field in its own Dispose(). No finalizer needed.
cards.deep: The full Dispose(bool disposing) pattern with GC.SuppressFinalize(this) is for unsealed classes that may have subclasses, and for classes that hold an unmanaged resource directly. For the latter there's SafeHandle, the next lesson.

cards.q: A class stores a FileStream in a field. What's the right move?
options: Implement IDisposable and call _file.Dispose() in Dispose()
Write a finalizer that closes the file
Nothing: the GC will close it
cards.explain: The owner of a resource passes the responsibility up: its callers will wrap it in using too.

cards.q: What is true? Select all that apply.
options: Dispose() releases the resource right away, without waiting for the GC
After Dispose() the object may still live in memory
using calls Dispose() even on an exception
Dispose() frees the object's memory
Every class needs IDisposable
cards.explain: Dispose closes the OS resource. The object's own memory is still freed by the GC once the object becomes unreachable.

lessons.title: SafeHandle and leaks
lessons.sub: Native handles and objects that won't die

cards.title: When the resource is fully native
cards.body:
Sometimes P/Invoke hands you a raw OS handle, just an IntPtr number. It must be closed even if someone forgot to call Dispose.

You don't need to write your own finalizer for that: .NET has a ready-made wrapper, SafeHandle.

cards.title: Why SafeHandle beats your own finalizer
cards.body:
Its finalizer is critical: the runtime runs it with stronger guarantees than a regular one.

While a P/Invoke call is in progress, SafeHandle counts references, so the handle can't be closed mid-call. Otherwise the OS could hand the same number to another resource, and data would go to the wrong place (handle recycling).

All you have to write is ReleaseHandle().

cards.q: Why is closing a handle in the middle of a P/Invoke call dangerous?
options: The OS may give the same number to a new resource, and the code writes data to the wrong place
The program gets slower
It isn't dangerous
cards.explain: Handle numbers get reused. SafeHandle won't let a handle close while a call is using it.

cards.q: What in .NET already uses SafeHandle?
options: FileStream, sockets and other wrappers over OS resources
Only your code
Nothing, it's an obsolete class
cards.explain: SafeFileHandle, SafeSocketHandle, SafeWaitHandle: all of them derive from SafeHandle.

cards.title: Leaks happen even with a GC
cards.body:
The GC only removes what's unreachable. If something alive references an object you no longer need, that object will never die.

The classic case is subscribing to an event on a long-lived object. The event keeps a reference to the subscriber.
cards.code:
AppEvents.Changed += window.OnChanged;
// the window was closed, but never unsubscribed

cards.task: The window was closed: form.window = null. Run a collection and see whether Window dies. Then fix the leak.

cards.q: The window was closed, but memory keeps growing. The profiler shows a static event holding the window. What do you do?
options: Unsubscribe from the event when the window closes
Call GC.Collect()
Add a finalizer to the window
cards.explain: As long as the event references the window, the window is reachable. Neither GC.Collect nor a finalizer will help.

cards.q: What can keep an unneeded object alive? Select all that apply.
options: A subscription to an event on a long-lived object
A static cache collection that is never cleared
A timer that references the object
A local variable of a method that already returned
A reference cycle between two garbage objects
cards.explain: A leak in .NET is always a path from a root to an object you don't need. Finished methods and garbage cycles don't create such a path.

cards.q: Someone forgot Dispose on an object with a SafeHandle. What happens next?
items: The object becomes unreachable
The GC finds it and puts it on the finalization queue
The finalizer thread calls ReleaseHandle()
The next collection frees the memory
cards.explain: The resource does get released, just late. Dispose is always better.

lessons.title: Final: the big cleanup
lessons.sub: GC, finalizers and resources: test yourself

cards.task: Clean up everything: the session with its cart, and the logger with its finalizer.

cards.q: An object is in Gen 2. A Gen 0 collection just ran. What happened to it?
options: Nothing
It was removed
It moved to Gen 3
cards.explain: A Gen 0 collection doesn't look at older generations. And there is no Gen 3.

cards.q: What counts as a root? Select all that apply.
options: A static field
A local variable of a running method
A field of a garbage object
An object in Gen 2
cards.explain: A generation doesn't make an object a root. Roots are thread stacks and static fields.

cards.q: From what size does an object go to the LOH?
options: 85,000 bytes and up
1 KB and up
1 MB and up
Only string arrays
cards.explain: The LOH threshold is 85,000 bytes.

cards.q: The connection must close even if Count throws an exception
cards.explain: using var calls Dispose at the end of the block, however you leave it.

cards.q: Why is SafeHandle better than your own finalizer?
options: Critical finalization and protection against closing a handle mid-call
It opens files faster
It isn't needed in .NET 8
cards.explain: SafeHandle closes the handle reliably and won't let the number be reused while a call is in progress.

cards.q: A references B, B references A, and nothing else references them. What happens during a collection?
options: Both are removed
Both stay forever
Only A is removed
cards.explain: They can't be reached from the roots, so they're garbage. The cycle doesn't save them.

cards.q: Where is the memory leak here?
cards.explain: Market is static and lives forever. The subscription holds on to every PriceView. You need to unsubscribe, for example in Dispose().

cards.q: An object with a finalizer became garbage. What's the minimum number of collections before its memory is freed?
options: Two
One
None
cards.explain: The first puts it on the finalization queue, the second frees it.

cards.q: Match them up

units.title: Threads and the thread pool
units.blurb: Threads and the scheduler, data races, lock and Interlocked, deadlock, the thread pool and its starvation. You switch the threads yourself and catch the bugs.

lessons.title: A thread is a worker
lessons.sub: Threads, cores and the OS scheduler

cards.title: Several things at once
cards.body:
A thread is a worker that walks through code line by line. Every program has at least one, the main thread.

You can create more threads, and they will run at the same time: on different CPU cores, or taking turns on one.

cards.title: Who decides who runs
cards.body:
Threads are managed by the OS scheduler. It lets a thread run for a short time slice and can switch to another at any moment, even in the middle of a line of code.

Picture two cooks in one kitchen: the head chef decides who does what, and can interrupt either of them mid-sentence.
cards.deep: A time slice is on the order of tens of milliseconds; a context switch costs microseconds. On a machine with N cores, at most N threads truly run at once.

cards.q: What gets printed first?
options: Unknown: the scheduler decides
Always "from Main"
Always "from thread"
cards.explain: After Start(), the two threads run independently. The output order can change from run to run.

cards.task: You are the scheduler. Two threads do count++, and you decide whose step is next. Run both threads to completion.

cards.q: What is true about threads? Select all that apply.
options: Each thread has its own stack
The heap is shared by all threads
The scheduler can interrupt a thread at any moment
Threads run strictly in the order they were created
More threads is always faster
cards.explain: Separate stacks and a shared heap follow straight from the memory unit. Extra threads just get in each other's way.

cards.q: How expensive is creating a thread?
options: Noticeably: stack memory plus OS work, which is why threads get reused
It costs nothing
Cheaper than calling a method
cards.explain: Each thread needs its own stack, typically around a megabyte of address space, plus system structures. That's why the thread pool exists (lesson 4).

cards.title: A shared heap is a source of trouble
cards.body:
Each thread has its own local variables: they live on its stack. But objects on the heap are shared.

If two threads change the same object at once, the result can break. How exactly is the next lesson.

cards.q: Two threads run the same method with a local variable int i. How many i variables are there?
options: Two: each thread has its own stack and its own frame
One shared variable
It depends on the scheduler
cards.explain: Every method call gets its own frame on its own thread's stack.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A worker that walks through code

lessons.title: Data races
lessons.sub: Why count++ from two threads loses increments

cards.title: count++ is three actions
cards.body: To the CPU, count++ is three steps: read count from memory, add 1, write it back. Remember CIL from the first unit? Here it is:
cards.code:
ldsfld  int32 Program::count   // read
ldc.i4.1
add                            // add
stsfld  int32 Program::count   // write

cards.task: Two threads do count++. Pick an order of steps so that count ends up equal to 1.

cards.q: Why did we get 1 and not 2?
options: Both threads read 0 before anyone wrote 1
The CPU can't add from two threads
The second thread never started
cards.explain: Each added 1 to the 0 it had read and wrote 1. The second increment overwrote the first.

cards.task: Now for real: two threads each do count++ 1,000 times. Run it a few times and look at the results.

cards.q: Why is the result different every time and almost never 2,000?
options: Thread switches land at different moments
count++ has a random number generator inside
There isn't enough memory
cards.explain: An increment is lost only when a switch happens between the read and the write. That happens more often on some runs, less on others.

cards.title: This is called a data race
cards.body:
A race condition is when the result depends on how threads happened to switch.

These are the nastiest bugs: everything works on the developer's machine, but on a loaded server it breaks once a week. The debugger often "cures" a race because it changes the timing.

cards.q: Where can a race happen? Select all that apply.
options: Two threads add items to the same List<T>
Two threads do total += x on a shared field
One thread checks if (cache == null) while another is filling it
Each thread sums into its own local variable
Two threads only read an immutable string
cards.explain: A race needs shared mutable memory and at least one write. Your own local variables and reading immutable data are safe.

cards.q: This method is called from many threads. Where is the race?
cards.explain: _hits is a shared static field, and ++ is three steps. local belongs to each thread separately.

cards.q: Two threads add to the same List<T> without synchronization. What can happen?
options: Lost items or an exception: List<T> isn't thread-safe
Nothing, List<T> synchronizes itself
The items just end up shuffled
cards.explain: Add has several steps inside too: check the size, write, bump the counter. A race breaks them. That's what ConcurrentQueue, ConcurrentDictionary or lock are for.

lessons.title: lock, Interlocked and deadlock
lessons.sub: How to fix races without hanging the program

cards.title: lock: one at a time
cards.body: lock (obj) { … } lets only one thread into the block. The others wait at the door until it leaves.
cards.deep: lock is Monitor.Enter/Exit inside try/finally. Since .NET 9 and C# 13 there's a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type, and lock on it is more efficient. Don't do lock(this) or lock on a string: other code can reach those objects and take the same lock.

cards.task: Same count++, but inside a lock. Try to get 1 again, then run both threads to completion.

cards.q: Why couldn't you lose an increment with lock?
options: While A is inside the lock, B can't start its steps
lock makes the CPU faster
lock runs threads one after another from the start of the program
cards.explain: Inside the lock, the read, add and write run as one chunk relative to other threads using the same lock.

cards.title: Interlocked: atomic, no lock needed
cards.body: For simple number operations there's Interlocked: Increment, Add, Exchange, CompareExchange. The CPU runs them as a single indivisible instruction, faster than a lock.
cards.code: Interlocked.Increment(ref count);

cards.task: Interlocked.Increment: run 2 threads × 1,000 and check the result.

cards.q: What do 2 threads × 1,000 calls to Interlocked.Increment give you?
options: Always 2,000
A different number around 2,000 each time
Always 1,000
cards.explain: Read, add and write are one indivisible operation. You can't lose an increment.

cards.title: The price of locks: deadlock
cards.body:
If a thread needs two locks and another thread takes the same locks in the opposite order, they can get stuck forever: each waits for the lock the other holds.

That's a deadlock. The program doesn't crash. It just hangs.

cards.task: A takes L1, then L2. B does the opposite. Drive the threads into a deadlock.
Fix it: make both threads take the locks in the same order. Then run them to completion.

cards.q: What's the main rule against lock deadlocks?
options: Always take locks in the same order
Take as many locks at once as you can
Add Thread.Sleep before lock
cards.explain: With a single order, the second thread waits on the first lock and can't grab the second one. No waiting cycle forms.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: One thread in the block, the rest wait
An indivisible operation on a number
Threads wait for each other forever
The result depends on thread switches

lessons.title: The thread pool
lessons.sub: Ready-made threads and a work queue

cards.title: Why a pool
cards.body:
Creating a thread for every small task is expensive. The thread pool (ThreadPool) keeps a set of ready threads: tasks join a queue, and a free thread picks up the next one.

Task.Run, timers and continuations after await all run on the pool.
cards.code:
Task.Run(() => Compress(file));
ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(_ => Log("done"));

cards.task: Add 16 CPU tasks and start the clock. Watch the threads work through the queue.

cards.q: How many threads does the pool have at startup?
options: Usually one per logical CPU core
One
A thousand
As many as there are queued tasks
cards.explain: By default the pool's minimum thread count equals the number of logical processors. From there the pool grows as needed.

cards.title: The pool grows carefully
cards.body: If every thread is busy and the queue is stuck, the pool adds a thread, but gradually, not all at once. Too many threads is bad too: they get in each other's way and eat memory.
cards.deep: The thread count is tuned by a hill-climbing algorithm: the pool tries adding or removing a thread and checks whether throughput went up. ThreadPool.SetMinThreads is a crutch that hides the problem instead of solving it.

cards.q: Why doesn't the pool create 1,000 threads right away for 1,000 tasks?
options: Threads are expensive and there are few cores anyway: extra threads would just keep switching
Windows forbids it
The pool can't count to 1,000
cards.explain: On 8 cores, at most 8 threads run at once. The rest would burn time on switches and memory on stacks.

cards.q: What runs on the thread pool? Select all that apply.
options: Task.Run(…)
The continuation after await in a console app and ASP.NET Core
A System.Threading.Timer callback
Code on the WPF UI thread
new Thread(…).Start()
cards.explain: The UI thread is a separate thread of its own. new Thread creates a new thread outside the pool.

cards.q: A pool task spends 10 minutes building a report. What's wrong with that?
options: It ties up a pool thread for a long time; long tasks are better on a dedicated thread (TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning)
Nothing
The pool kills it after a minute
cards.explain: The pool is built for short tasks. A long one holds a thread, and the pool has to ramp up to compensate.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A dedicated thread you create yourself
Ready threads with a shared queue
Runs one thread at any given moment

lessons.title: Thread pool starvation
lessons.sub: .Result, Thread.Sleep and why a thread shouldn't wait

cards.title: A waiting thread is a wasted thread
cards.body:
If code on the pool calls .Result, .Wait() or Thread.Sleep, the thread just sits there doing nothing while it waits for the network or disk.

Tie up every thread like that, and new tasks pile up in the queue. That's thread pool starvation.

cards.task: Add 16 requests that wait on the network via .Result and start the clock. See how many threads are stuck and how the pool grows.

cards.q: The pool keeps adding threads, but the queue still doesn't move. Why?
options: The new threads also pick up .Result requests and start waiting too
The pool is broken
.Result requests run one at a time
cards.explain: As long as the code blocks the thread, every new thread just becomes one more waiter.

cards.title: What if we don't block?
cards.body:
With await, the thread doesn't wait for the network: it sends the request and goes straight back to the pool for the next task.

When the response arrives, the continuation joins the queue and runs on any free thread.

cards.task: Compare: add 16 requests that use await and look at the thread count and the average wait.

cards.q: What did the rig show?
options: With await the same threads serve more requests: while the network wait is on, the thread is free
await downloads data from the network faster
await creates a new thread for every request
cards.explain: The network didn't get faster. The thread just works on other requests while there's no response yet.

wrong.2: The opposite: await doesn't create threads. Waiting on the network doesn't occupy a thread at all.

cards.q: What can cause thread pool starvation? Select all that apply.
options: .Result and .Wait() on tasks doing network calls
Thread.Sleep in code running on the pool
A synchronous read from a slow disk in every request
await httpClient.GetAsync(…)
Short computations with no waiting
cards.explain: Anything that holds a pool thread without doing work. await and short computations don't hold the thread.

cards.q: An ASP.NET Core server: under load, responses suddenly lag by seconds, yet the CPU is nearly idle. What do you suspect first?
options: Thread pool starvation: blocking calls like .Result somewhere
Not enough RAM
A slow JIT
cards.explain: An idle CPU with growing latency is the classic sign: the threads exist, but they're stuck waiting.

cards.title: A bridge to async/await
cards.body:
Threads, the pool and locking are the foundation of async/await. Next up: what the compiler does with await, where the code continues, and where the infamous .Result deadlock in UI apps comes from.

That's a separate course, "Async/await in depth". You'll find it in the catalog.
cards.deep: Since .NET 6 the pool compensates faster for blocking on Task.Wait and .Result by adding a thread right away. That eases the symptoms but doesn't cure them. A blocked thread still sits idle and eats memory, and under heavy load the compensation isn't enough.

lessons.title: Final: many threads
lessons.sub: Races, locks and the pool: test yourself

cards.task: Show a lost update: get count to end at 1.

cards.q: What steps make up count++?
items: Read count from memory
Add 1 in a register
Write the result to memory
cards.explain: Three separate steps, and the thread can be interrupted between any of them.

cards.task: Fix the deadlock and run both threads to completion.

cards.q: What do threads share? Select all that apply.
options: The heap
Static fields
The stack
A method's local variables
cards.explain: Each thread has its own stack and everything on it.

cards.q: You just need to count requests from many threads. What do you pick?
options: Interlocked.Increment
A lock around the whole request handler
Nothing, ++ is atomic
cards.explain: Interlocked solves it with a single instruction and makes nobody wait.

cards.q: Which line is bad practice?
cards.explain: Anyone who uses the object has a reference to it and can take the same lock. A private readonly lock object is better.

cards.q: The CPU is idle, yet requests sit in the pool queue. Most likely…
options: Pool threads are blocked waiting
The CPU is too slow
The garbage collector is turned off
cards.explain: Thread pool starvation: the threads exist, but they're waiting instead of working.

cards.task: Serve 8 requests without a single thread stuck waiting.

cards.q: Two threads read the same immutable string. Do you need synchronization?
options: No: races only happen when something writes
Yes, always
Only on ARM
cards.explain: If nobody changes the data, any number of threads can read it.

cards.q: Match them up

units.title: Assemblies and versions
units.blurb: What an assembly holds, its three versions and which one the loader checks, strong names and the GAC then and now, deps.json instead of folder probing, and how NuGet settles on one package version.

lessons.title: Inside an assembly
lessons.sub: Manifest, modules, resources and type forwarding

cards.title: An assembly is more than a file
cards.body:
In the unit "How .NET code runs" you saw that a .dll holds CIL and metadata. Now something else matters more: an assembly is the unit of deployment and versioning. It has an identity made of four parts: simple name, version, culture and public key.

A type belongs to an assembly. To the CLR, Shop.Order from the Shop assembly and Shop.Order from the Shop.Legacy assembly are two different types, even though the names match.
cards.deep:
This explains a famous puzzle: InvalidCastException: Unable to cast object of type 'Shop.Order' to type 'Shop.Order'. It means the same assembly got loaded twice (say, from two paths or into two load contexts): the full type name matches, the type does not. How assemblies end up in different contexts is the topic of the next unit.

PublicKeyToken=null means the assembly has no strong name. Strong names are lesson 3.

cards.title: The manifest: the assembly passport
cards.body:
The manifest is the part of the metadata that describes the assembly as a whole rather than individual types. It is a few tables:

  • Assembly — its own identity: name, version, culture, public key;
  • AssemblyRef — which assemblies it depends on and which versions it expects;
  • ManifestResource — embedded resources;
  • ExportedType — types the assembly hands over to another assembly;
  • File — other files of the assembly (needed by multi-file assemblies).

This is how a manifest looks in a disassembler:
cards.deep: The .ver line in .assembly extern is the version the compiler built your code against. It wrote it into AssemblyRef for good: you can rebuild the dependency, but the reference inside Shop.dll stays 9.0.0.0 until you rebuild Shop itself. What the loader does with that number is lesson 2.

cards.q: What makes up an assembly identity?
options: Name, version, culture and public key
File name and build date
Name, AssemblyVersion and FileVersion
File path and IL hash
cards.explain: These four parts are stored in the Assembly table and in every AssemblyRef. File name, path and date are not part of the identity.
