wrong.2: FileVersion is a resource for Windows Explorer and is not part of the identity. More in lesson 2.

cards.title: Modules: then and now
cards.body:
A module is one PE file with metadata. An assembly consists of modules, and one of them holds the manifest.

Then. In .NET Framework an assembly could span several files: csc -target:module produced a .netmodule file without a manifest, and the File table of the main module listed the others with their hashes. This let you glue code in different languages into one assembly or download rarely used parts over the network.

Now. Modern .NET does not support multi-file assemblies: one assembly, one module, one file. Single-file publishing is an entirely different mechanism, covered in the next unit.
cards.deep: Every module has its own <Module> type in the metadata — it holds global functions and the module initializer ([ModuleInitializer] in C# 9). Metadata is addressed by tokens scoped to a module, so references between modules of one assembly went through a separate ModuleRef table. In modern projects this legacy barely shows up.

cards.q: What does every modern .NET assembly have? Select all.
options: A manifest with its identity
Exactly one module — the file itself
Metadata
Embedded resources
A .netmodule file next to it
cards.explain: Resources are optional. .netmodule files were part of multi-file assemblies in .NET Framework; the modern runtime does not load them.

cards.title: Resources inside an assembly
cards.body:
For a file with the EmbeddedResource build action, the compiler puts its bytes right into the PE file and its name into the ManifestResource table. The name is built like this: the project root namespace, the file path with dots, the file name.

You read a resource as a stream, without unpacking it to disk.
cards.deep:
.resx files are compiled into binary .resources and embedded the same way; ResourceManager reads them.

Translations go into satellite assemblies: ru/Shop.resources.dll. Such an assembly has culture ru in its identity and contains no code — only resources. ResourceManager looks for the assembly of the current UI culture, then of its parent culture, and finally falls back to the resources in the main assembly.

cards.q: Print the names of all embedded resources and open each one
cards.explain: Names come from the ManifestResource table; the stream reads the resource bytes from the PE file. GetFiles is about the files of a multi-file assembly and has nothing to do with embedded resources.

cards.title: Version 2: a type moves to another assembly
cards.body:
In version 2 the Money class moves from Shop.dll to the new Shop.Core.dll. The old app was not rebuilt, and its IL says [Shop]Shop.Money: the CLR looks for the type in Shop, does not find it — TypeLoadException.

The fix is type forwarding. Shop.dll references Shop.Core and declares an attribute. The compiler writes a row into the ExportedType table, and the CLR, failing to find the type in Shop, follows that row.
cards.deep:
The whole modern BCL relies on forwarding. Your code is compiled against System.Runtime, but at run time System.Runtime.dll is an almost empty assembly that forwards Object, String and the rest to System.Private.CoreLib. netstandard.dll from the history course works the same way: a facade that on each platform forwards types to wherever they really live.

The opposite attribute, TypeForwardedFrom, is not for the loader but for serializers that stored the old assembly name in their data.

cards.q: Money moved from Shop.dll to Shop.Core.dll without TypeForwardedTo. The old App.exe was not rebuilt. What happens?
options: TypeLoadException once the Money type is needed
It works: the CLR finds the type by name in any loaded assembly
App.exe will not start: a verification error at process start
Money is loaded from an old copy of Shop.dll in a cache
cards.explain: A type reference in IL includes the assembly. The CLR looks for Money only in Shop and fails as soon as the JIT compiles a method that needs that type.

wrong.1: There is no such "search every assembly": the assembly name is part of the type reference.

cards.q: The manifest of Shop.dll version 2. Which line lets old code find Money?
cards.explain: .class extern forwarder is a row of the ExportedType table: "look for Shop.Money in Shop.Core". The TypeForwardedTo attribute creates it.

cards.title: Reference assemblies: compile against one, run another
cards.body:
The compiler needs only signatures, not method bodies. That is what reference assemblies are: the same public types and methods, but with throw null instead of bodies.

Your project is compiled against reference assemblies from the Microsoft.NETCore.App.Ref pack and runs against the real assemblies of the installed runtime. The only link between them is the identity: name and version in AssemblyRef.
cards.code:
// what a method looks like in a reference assembly
public static int Parse(string s) => throw null;
cards.deep: A reference assembly carries ReferenceAssemblyAttribute, and the runtime refuses to execute it: BadImageFormatException. The SDK builds a reference assembly for your own projects too (obj/…/ref/): if the public API did not change, dependent projects are not recompiled. That is where fast incremental builds in large solutions come from.

cards.q: Match the manifest table to what it holds
pairs: A dependency and the version it was built against
A type forwarded to another assembly
Other modules of a multi-file assembly

lessons.title: Three assembly versions
lessons.sub: Which one the loader looks at — and where that leads

cards.title: One number in the project, four in the output
cards.body:
A library actually has several versions, and they live in different places:

  • AssemblyVersion — in the metadata, part of the identity. The compiler also writes it into the AssemblyRef of every consumer;
  • FileVersion — in the Win32 VERSIONINFO resource; Explorer shows it in the file properties;
  • InformationalVersion — an attribute with a free-form string: the product version;
  • PackageVersion — in the package .nuspec; only NuGet sees it.

In an SDK project you usually set a single Version property, and the SDK derives the rest from it.
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <Version>2.4.1-beta.2</Version>
</PropertyGroup>
<!-- the SDK derives:
     AssemblyVersion      2.4.1.0
     FileVersion          2.4.1.0
     InformationalVersion 2.4.1-beta.2+a1b2c3d
     PackageVersion       2.4.1-beta.2 -->
cards.deep:
The SDK generates the attributes into obj/…/Shop.AssemblyInfo.cs (the GenerateAssemblyInfo property). The +a1b2c3d suffix is the commit hash: starting with the .NET 8 SDK, Source Link is built in and appends it to InformationalVersion by default. Turn it off with IncludeSourceRevisionInInformationalVersion=false.

Each of the four parts is a 16-bit number; in AssemblyVersion it is at most 65,534. A CI build number like 70,000 does not fit there.

cards.q: Match the version to who reads it
pairs: The CLR loader: part of the identity
Windows Explorer in the file properties
People: a product string with the commit hash

cards.title: AssemblyVersion gets baked into the consumer
cards.body:
The app was built against Shop 2.4.1.0 — its manifest now permanently says .assembly extern Shop { .ver 2:4:1:0 }. Later Shop.dll in the folder is replaced with a new one. Whether the runtime accepts it is decided by comparing this number with the version of the assembly it found.

The other versions are only read by code, explicitly:
cards.deep: The old trick AssemblyVersion("1.0.*") — a version made from the build date and time — gives error CS8357 in SDK projects: deterministic compilation (Deterministic, on by default) is incompatible with wildcards. And that is good: a version that changes on every build would break binding of strong-named assemblies in .NET Framework. Also note that in a single-file app Location is an empty string, so FileVersionInfo cannot be read this way.

cards.q: Which version does the CLR loader compare when it looks for a dependency?
options: AssemblyVersion
FileVersion
InformationalVersion
The NuGet package version
cards.explain: Only AssemblyVersion is part of the identity and is stored in AssemblyRef. The loader needs none of the others.

wrong.1: FileVersion is a Win32 resource for Explorer. The CLR loader does not compare it.
wrong.3: The package version stays in NuGet. It never gets into the assembly or into AssemblyRef.

cards.title: Then: exact match. Now: no lower
cards.body:
.NET Framework requires an exact match of the AssemblyRef version for a strong-named assembly. A different one is found — FileLoadException ("The located assembly's manifest definition does not match the assembly reference"), unless the configuration has a binding redirect. For an assembly without a strong name, Framework does not check the version at all.

.NET Core and .NET 5+ have no strict binding: an assembly with a version no lower than requested is fine. Lower — the same FileLoadException.

  • requested 12.0.0.0, found 13.0.0.0: Framework — error (without a redirect), .NET 8 — loads;
  • requested 13.0.0.0, found 12.0.0.0: an error everywhere.
cards.deep: You rely on this rule every day: an app built for net8.0 references System.Runtime 8.0.0.0, and when it runs on runtime 9 (via rollForward) it gets System.Runtime 9.0.0.0 — and that is fine. In Framework, the same problem for its own assemblies was solved by "unification": references to any version of the system assemblies were automatically mapped to the version of the installed Framework.

cards.q: The Reports library was built against Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.0.0. The folder of a .NET 8 app holds Newtonsoft.Json with AssemblyVersion 13.0.0.0. What happens?
options: 13.0.0.0 loads: the version is no lower than requested
FileLoadException: the version does not match
A binding redirect in app.config is required
Both versions load side by side
cards.explain: The modern loader accepts a version no lower than requested. Whether 13 is compatible with code built against 12 is the library author's responsibility.

wrong.1: That is what .NET Framework would do with a strong-named assembly.
wrong.2: The modern runtime does not read binding redirects from app.config: it does not need them.

cards.title: Why library AssemblyVersions are "round"
cards.body:
Microsoft guidance for libraries: keep only the major version in AssemblyVersion. Packages 3.0, 3.1 and 3.7.2 get AssemblyVersion 3.0.0.0, version 4 gets 4.0.0.0. This way Framework consumers need binding redirects less often. The CI build number goes into FileVersion, where it bothers nobody.

But do not freeze AssemblyVersion forever: then only one version fits in the GAC, and an update breaks everyone who references it.
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <Version>3.7.2</Version>
  <AssemblyVersion>3.0.0.0</AssemblyVersion>
  <FileVersion>3.7.2.41</FileVersion>
</PropertyGroup>
cards.deep: This scheme has a price in modern .NET. The app was built against 3.7.2, but deployment put 3.5.0 into the folder — both have AssemblyVersion 3.0.0.0, and the "no lower" check silently passes. If the code calls a method added in 3.7, you get MissingMethodException when the JIT compiles the calling method instead of a clear load error. Restore protects you here: NuGet will not drop a package below the required version without warning NU1605. But it does not see a file copied into the folder by hand.

cards.q: GenerateAssemblyInfo is off and you write the attributes yourself. Fill in: identity, file number with the CI build number, product string
cards.explain: If you leave GenerateAssemblyInfo on and write these attributes by hand, the compiler reports CS0579: duplicate attribute. Usually versions are set with properties in the .csproj.

cards.title: Version 2: "no lower" does not mean "compatible"
cards.body:
The loader checks only the number. It does not look inside. In version 3.1 the Shop author removed Order.Total() and kept AssemblyVersion 3.0.0.0. Reports.dll was built against 3.0 and calls Total.

The assembly loads without errors. It fails later — MissingMethodException when the JIT compiles the method containing that call. That is why breaking changes ship only in a new major version: SemVer is a contract the runtime will not check for you.

cards.q: What does the .NET 8 loader check about a dependency it found?
options: The name, and that the version is no lower than requested
That the set of public methods matches what was expected
That FileVersion matches the one stored in the reference
The strong-name signature
cards.explain: The loader does not check API compatibility, the reference does not store FileVersion, and the modern runtime never validates the strong-name signature.

cards.q: The About window needs the version with the beta suffix. Which line gives it?
cards.explain: Suffixes like -beta.2 and the commit hash exist only in InformationalVersion. AssemblyVersion and FileVersion are four numbers, and ImageRuntimeVersion is the metadata format version, which for modern assemblies is "v4.0.30319".

cards.q: What is true about versions? Select all.
options: FileVersion can change on every CI build with no effect on consumers
Changing the AssemblyVersion of a strong-named assembly requires redirects for .NET Framework consumers
InformationalVersion takes part in binding on .NET 8
On .NET 8 an assembly whose AssemblyVersion is lower than in the reference will not load
The NuGet package version is written into the consumer's AssemblyRef
cards.explain: Of all the versions, binding looks only at AssemblyVersion. The package version lives in NuGet and never gets into the assembly.

lessons.title: Strong names and the GAC
lessons.sub: Signing, PublicKeyToken, binding redirects — then and now

cards.title: A name you cannot clash with by accident
cards.body:
Two vendors can each ship their own Utils.dll. By simple name you cannot tell them apart. A strong name adds the author's public key to the name, version and culture.

At build time the compiler hashes the file and signs the hash with the private RSA key. The public key goes into the manifest, the signature into a separate area of the PE file. A consumer stores a short fingerprint of the key in AssemblyRef — the PublicKeyToken, 8 bytes.
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <SignAssembly>true</SignAssembly>
  <AssemblyOriginatorKeyFile>Shop.snk</AssemblyOriginatorKeyFile>
</PropertyGroup>
<!-- the key pair is created by sn -k Shop.snk -->
cards.deep:
The PublicKeyToken is the last 8 bytes of the SHA-1 hash of the public key, in reverse order (ECMA-335, section II.6.2.1.3). The full name of a signed assembly: Shop, Version=1.2.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=….

Open-source projects that do not want to expose the private key have public signing (PublicSign): only the public key goes into the assembly, and the signature is not real. The identity is the same, but the assembly is not "signed" in the cryptographic sense. A similar trick is delay signing: the real signature is applied later, on a secured machine.

cards.q: What does a consumer store in the AssemblyRef of a strong-named dependency?
options: Name, version, culture and PublicKeyToken
The whole public key and the dependency's signature
The author's private key
FileVersion and the file path
cards.explain: A reference needs only the identity. Instead of the full public key, compilers write its 8-byte fingerprint.

wrong.2: The private key never leaves the author — otherwise the signature would be meaningless.

cards.title: Then: the GAC and the answer to DLL hell
cards.body:
In the history course you saw DLL hell: a new program overwrites a shared DLL, and an old one breaks. .NET Framework answered with the Global Assembly Cache (GAC) — a shared store that admits only strong-named assemblies.

Since the identity includes the version and the key, Shop 1.0 and Shop 2.0 live side by side in the GAC, and each app gets the one it was built against. Hence strict binding: a reference to 1.0.0.0 loads only 1.0.0.0.

One more Framework rule: strong naming is "viral" — a signed assembly can reference only signed ones.
cards.code:
gacutil /i Shop.dll
:: .NET Framework 4.x: C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\assembly\
:: before 4.0:         C:\Windows\assembly\
cards.deep:
A strong name is identity, not protection. Starting with .NET Framework 3.5 SP1, the signature of fully trusted assemblies is usually not verified at load time (strong-name bypass) — it is verified when installing into the GAC. To prove who wrote the code, use Authenticode and NuGet package signing.

That is why Microsoft even recommends that open-source libraries keep the key pair right in the repository — Newtonsoft.Json and NodaTime, for example, do so.

cards.q: What did a strong name give you in .NET Framework? Select all.
options: The right to put the assembly into the GAC
Two versions of one assembly side by side
The ability to reference the assembly from other signed assemblies
A guarantee that this very author wrote the code
Faster JIT compilation
cards.explain: The strong-name signature has long gone unverified during normal loading, and the keys of many libraries are public. It is an identity, not an author certificate.

cards.title: How Framework found an assembly
cards.body:
When code needed a dependency, the .NET Framework loader (called Fusion) went step by step:

  • configuration: binding redirects from app.config, publisher policy from the GAC, machine.config — these may change the requested version;
  • already loaded? — then return it;
  • the GAC — for strong-named assemblies only;
  • codeBase from the configuration, or probing: the app folder, a subfolder named after the assembly, folders from <probing privatePath>, first .dll, then .exe.
cards.deep: Probing tries paths like [folder]/Shop.dll, [folder]/Shop/Shop.dll, [folder]/[privatePath]/Shop.dll, [folder]/[privatePath]/Shop/Shop.dll. The file found is checked against the reference: name, key, version. A mismatch gives FileLoadException with HRESULT 0x80131040; nothing found gives FileNotFoundException. You debugged this with the Fusion log: fuslogvw.exe showed every path it tried.

cards.q: Put the .NET Framework assembly lookup steps in order
items: Apply redirects and policy from configuration
Check whether it is already loaded
Look in the GAC
Probe the app folders
cards.explain: First the configuration decides which version to look for, then already loaded assemblies, the GAC, and only at the end the disk next to the app. That is why an assembly in the GAC beats a copy in the bin folder.

cards.title: Binding redirects
cards.body:
Strict binding requires the exact version. But Reports.dll was built against Newtonsoft.Json 12, Charts.dll against 13, and the folder can hold only one file. The way out is a binding redirect: "load every version in this range as 13.0.0.0".

You do not have to write them by hand: in Framework app projects, MSBuild with AutoGenerateBindingRedirects adds them to App.exe.config at build time.
cards.code:
<runtime>
  <assemblyBinding xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v1">
    <dependentAssembly>
      <assemblyIdentity name="Newtonsoft.Json"
                        publicKeyToken="30ad4fe6b2a6aeed" culture="neutral" />
      <bindingRedirect oldVersion="0.0.0.0-13.0.0.0" newVersion="13.0.0.0" />
    </dependentAssembly>
  </assemblyBinding>
</runtime>
cards.deep: Publisher policy is the same redirect, but from the library author: a separate signed assembly policy.1.0.Shop.dll in the GAC. This is how Microsoft shipped fixes to shared components without touching app configuration. An app could opt out with <publisherPolicy apply="no"/>.

cards.q: Complete the redirect: load any version up to 13 as 13.0.0.0
cards.code:
<dependentAssembly>
  <assemblyIdentity name="Newtonsoft.Json"
                    ___="30ad4fe6b2a6aeed" culture="neutral" />
  <bindingRedirect ___="0.0.0.0-13.0.0.0" ___="13.0.0.0" />
</dependentAssembly>
cards.explain: The assembly is identified by name, key token and culture. oldVersion is the range that references ask for; newVersion is what to load instead.

cards.title: Now: a strong name means almost nothing
cards.body:
In .NET Core and .NET 5+:

  • there is no GAC. Shared assemblies live in the folder of the installed runtime;
  • the runtime does not validate the strong-name signature and does not use it for binding;
  • binding redirects are not needed and are not read from app.config: a version no lower than requested loads.

Microsoft guidance for libraries: modern .NET only — signing is optional. If .NET Framework or .NET Standard is among the targets — sign all targets with one key. And never change the key: a new key is a new identity.
cards.deep: The compiler reports warning CS8002 when a signed assembly references an unsigned one. For libraries that target only .NET Core and .NET 5+ you can suppress it: a strong name gives nothing there. Another "do not" from the guidance: do not ship two packages, signed and unsigned (Contoso.Api and Contoso.Api.StrongNamed). To the CLR they are different assemblies and different types.

cards.q: A library targets only net8.0. Does it need a strong name?
options: Not necessarily: the modern runtime does not use strong names
Yes, otherwise .NET 8 will not load it
Yes, otherwise nuget.org will not accept the package
It must not: .NET 8 rejects signed assemblies
cards.explain: Strong names matter for .NET Framework and .NET Standard. For a library that targets only modern .NET it gives nothing — but does no harm either.

cards.q: A netstandard2.0 library is strong-named. The author lost the key and signed the new version with another one. What breaks?
options: .NET Framework apps: a different PublicKeyToken is a different identity, old references reject it
Nothing: the key is checked only when installing into the GAC
Only IDE hints
Every .NET 8 app stops loading it
cards.explain: The key token is part of the identity. To Framework this is a completely different assembly, and a redirect will not help: it redirects versions, not keys.

wrong.3: The modern runtime does not use the strong name for binding — nothing changes there.

cards.q: In a .NET Framework app one library references Newtonsoft.Json 9.0.0.0, another 12.0.0.0, and the folder has 13.0.0.0. Which line leaves one of the references without a redirect?
cards.code:
<dependentAssembly>
  <assemblyIdentity name="Newtonsoft.Json"
                    publicKeyToken="30ad4fe6b2a6aeed" culture="neutral" />
  <bindingRedirect oldVersion="0.0.0.0-11.0.0.0" newVersion="13.0.0.0" />
</dependentAssembly>
cards.explain: The range ends at 11.0.0.0: the reference to 9.0.0.0 is redirected, but the one to 12.0.0.0 is not, and loading fails with FileLoadException. The upper bound must be 13.0.0.0.

lessons.title: How .NET finds assemblies
lessons.sub: deps.json, the TPA and NuGet version rules

cards.title: Two JSON files instead of the GAC and probing
cards.body:
Build an app and two files appear next to App.dll:

  • App.runtimeconfig.json — which shared framework is needed (Microsoft.NETCore.App, Microsoft.AspNetCore.App) and which version, plus runtime settings;
  • App.deps.json — the full list of dependencies: which packages, which files from them, which versions.

In the unit "How .NET code runs" you saw that hostfxr and hostpolicy read them. How the host picks the runtime version is covered in the next unit. Here we look at what they say about assemblies.

cards.title: What deps.json holds
cards.body:
For each library it records what it depends on and which of its files are needed at run time. For assemblies from packages — the path inside the package and both versions: assemblyVersion and fileVersion.

The SDK writes this file at build time from the restore result. Nobody edits it by hand.
cards.deep: Further down the same file there is a "libraries" section: the kind of each entry (project or package), the sha512 hash of the package and its path in the NuGet cache. Packages with native or platform-specific parts also get "runtimeTargets" — files from runtimes/<rid>/ that the host picks for the current OS and architecture.

cards.q: What does deps.json store about an assembly from a NuGet package?
options: The path inside the package, assemblyVersion and fileVersion
Only the package name: the host finds the files itself
An IL hash of every method
The full path on the build machine
cards.explain: The path in deps.json is relative to the package root. The host computes the full path at startup: the app folder, the framework folders, extra probe paths.

cards.title: The TPA: a list instead of a disk walk
cards.body:
At startup the host turns the app deps.json and the framework deps.json into a list of full paths — the TPA (Trusted Platform Assemblies) — and hands it to the runtime. The next unit covers this chain in detail.

When code needs an assembly, the default context looks it up in the TPA by simple name — nobody walks the disk. Once found, the version is checked: no lower than requested (lesson 2).

Which raises a question: what if the same assembly is both in an app package and in the shared framework? Only one gets into the list — the one with the higher version.
cards.deep: The conflict is resolved twice. At build time the SDK (the ResolvePackageFileConflicts task) compares package files with framework files and drops the losers. At startup hostpolicy, while building the TPA, compares assemblyVersion and, on a tie, fileVersion. That is why deps.json stores both versions: this is the only place where FileVersion affects loading. You can see the outcome in the host trace (COREHOST_TRACE=1).

cards.q: A net9.0 app transitively gets the System.Text.Json 8.0.5 package. Which System.Text.Json assembly runs?
options: The one from the 9.0 shared framework: its version is higher
The one from package 8.0.5: the app package always wins
Both: each for its own consumers
Neither: the version conflict stops startup
cards.explain: In the 9.0 framework System.Text.Json has AssemblyVersion 9.0.0.0; package 8.0.5 has 8.0.0.0. The higher one wins, and code built against 8.0.0.0 accepts it: the version is no lower.

wrong.2: In the default context an assembly with a given name can have only one version.

cards.title: NuGet: one package version per project
cards.body:
Where does deps.json come from? From restore. NuGet walks the dependency graph, picks exactly one version of each package (per target framework of the project) and writes the result to obj/project.assets.json. From it the SDK adds references, copies files and writes deps.json.

The first rule is the lowest applicable version. Version="3.7.2" means "3.7.2 or higher", and NuGet takes the lowest available one, not the newest.
cards.code:
<ItemGroup>
  <PackageReference Include="Acme.Pricing" Version="3.7.2" />
  <PackageReference Include="Acme.Tax" Version="[2.0.0]" />
  <PackageReference Include="Acme.Log" Version="[1.0,2.0)" />
  <PackageReference Include="Acme.Feed" Version="5.*" />
</ItemGroup>
cards.deep:
Then: the packages.config format stored a flat list of all packages including transitive ones, conflicts were resolved at the moment each package was installed, and NuGet edited app.config and the .csproj itself. Now: PackageReference resolves the whole graph anew on every restore.

Floating versions like 5.* take the newest match — builds stop being reproducible. If you need them, turn on the packages.lock.json lock file (RestorePackagesWithLockFile).

cards.q: Match the version notation to its meaning
pairs: 3.7.2 or higher, the lowest available is taken

cards.title: Conflicts: direct dependencies and "cousins"
cards.body:
Several packages need the same package. Two rules:

  • Cousin dependencies: different branches require different minimums — NuGet takes the lowest version that satisfies everyone, i.e. the highest of the minimums;
  • Direct dependency wins: if a package version is specified closer to the root — say, in the project itself — it beats requirements deeper in the graph. Even if it is lower.

NuGet flags a downgrade with warning NU1605, and in SDK projects it is treated as an error by default. Incompatible requirements (exactly [1.4] and at least 1.6) give error NU1107 — then add a direct reference with the version you need.
cards.code:
App
├─ Acme.Pricing 3.7.2  →  Acme.Log >= 1.4
└─ Acme.Tax 2.0.0      →  Acme.Log >= 1.6
result: Acme.Log 1.6 — the lowest that satisfies both
cards.deep: Compare with npm: there each branch can have its own copy of a package. In .NET that is impossible by the nature of the runtime: in the default context an assembly with a given name loads once. So NuGet has to collapse the graph to one version, and compatibility rests on package authors following SemVer. Why exactly this version was chosen is shown by dotnet nuget why App.csproj Acme.Log (SDK 8.0.400 and later) or dotnet list package --include-transitive.

cards.q: App references Acme.Log 1.2 directly. Acme.Pricing, which App also depends on, requires Acme.Log 1.4 or higher. What does NuGet do?
options: Takes 1.2 and reports NU1605 — a downgrade
Takes 1.4: the package requirement is more important
Puts both versions into the project
Takes the newest version on the server
cards.explain: The direct dependency wins, even downward. NU1605 is an error by default in SDK projects, and rightly so: Acme.Pricing may call a method that does not exist in 1.2 yet.

cards.title: Central Package Management
cards.body:
In a solution of 40 projects the versions of one package drift apart quickly. Central Package Management (CPM) gathers them in a single Directory.Packages.props file at the repository root. Projects reference packages without a version.

  • CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled — raise transitive dependencies to the version in the file too. You cannot downgrade this way: error NU1109;
  • VersionOverride — an exception for a single project.
cards.code:
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Acme.Log" Version="1.6.0" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
cards.deep: Transitive pinning is handy for security patches: a vulnerable version came from deep in the graph, and you raise it with one line. But if your project is a library, NuGet writes the pinned packages as explicit dependencies at pack time, and consumers get them too. With more than one package source, CPM reports warning NU1507 and suggests setting up package source mapping.

cards.q: Turn on CPM: the version is set in one place, the project references the package without a version
cards.code:
<!-- Directory.Packages.props -->
<ItemGroup>
  <___ Include="Acme.Log" Version="1.6.0" />
</ItemGroup>

<!-- App.csproj -->
<ItemGroup>
  <___ Include="Acme.Log" />
</ItemGroup>
cards.explain: PackageVersion sets the version and does not add the package by itself. PackageReference adds it — without a Version attribute: with CPM on, restore reports an error if it is there.

cards.q: What is true about modern .NET and NuGet? Select all.
options: In a project, for one target framework, a package has exactly one version
Version="3.7.2" means "exactly 3.7.2"
The host takes the list of assemblies to run from deps.json
Transitive pinning in CPM can downgrade a version
project.assets.json is a restore output and is not committed to git
cards.explain: "3.7.2" is a lower bound; "exactly" is written as [3.7.2]. Transitive pinning only raises versions; an attempt to downgrade is error NU1109.

lessons.title: Final: assemblies and versions
lessons.sub: Identity, binding, strong names and NuGet

cards.q: A .NET Framework 4.8 app. A signed library was built against Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.0.0, the folder has 13.0.0.0, and App.exe.config has no redirect. What happens?
options: FileLoadException: strict binding requires 12.0.0.0
13.0.0.0 loads: the version is no lower than requested
Both versions load: each for its own consumers
A warning in the Fusion log, and the app carries on
cards.explain: For a strong-named assembly Framework requires an exact version match. The "no lower" rule belongs to .NET Core and .NET 5+.

wrong.1: That is how .NET 8 behaves, not Framework.

cards.q: Which of these change an assembly identity? Select all.
options: AssemblyVersion
The strong-name key
Culture
FileVersion
InformationalVersion
cards.explain: The identity is name, version, culture and public key. FileVersion and InformationalVersion are plain attributes; the CLR loader ignores them.

cards.q: A signed netstandard2.0 library. Which line should change so that 3.7.x patches do not require binding redirects for Framework consumers?
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <Version>3.7.2</Version>
  <AssemblyVersion>3.7.2.0</AssemblyVersion>
  <FileVersion>3.7.2.41</FileVersion>
  <SignAssembly>true</SignAssembly>
</PropertyGroup>
cards.explain: AssemblyVersion should be 3.0.0.0 — major only. Deleting the line is not enough: the SDK derives 3.7.2.0 from Version. Let the patch and CI build numbers live in Version and FileVersion.

cards.q: Acme.Pricing requires Acme.Log >= 2.1, Acme.Tax requires Acme.Log >= 2.0. The server has 2.0, 2.2 and 3.0, but no 2.1. What does NuGet pick?
options: Error NU1107
cards.explain: It needs the lowest version that satisfies both: at least 2.1. There is no 2.1, and the next available one is 2.2.

wrong.1: NuGet does not take the newest: the rule is the lowest applicable.
wrong.2: 2.0 does not satisfy Acme.Pricing.

cards.q: Put in order how a .NET 8 app gets the Acme.Log assembly
items: At build time the SDK writes App.deps.json from the restore result
hostfxr reads runtimeconfig.json and picks the framework
hostpolicy builds the TPA from the app and framework deps.json
Code touches a type from Acme.Log for the first time
The default context finds Acme.Log in the TPA by name and checks the version
cards.explain: First restore and build, then the host builds the assembly list, and only when the JIT meets a type from Acme.Log does the assembly load — by name from the list, with the "no lower" check.

cards.q: The Money class moved from Shop.dll to Shop.Core.dll. Make old programs find it
cards.code:
// Shop.dll, version 2
[assembly: ___(typeof(Shop.Money))]
cards.explain: TypeForwardedTo writes a row into ExportedType, and the CLR follows it to Shop.Core. TypeForwardedFrom goes on the type itself in the new assembly — serializers read it, not the loader.

cards.q: Match the .NET Framework mechanism to what became of it in modern .NET
pairs: Shared assemblies in the installed runtime folder
Not needed: a version no lower than requested fits
Lookup by name in the TPA list from deps.json

cards.q: A colleague says: "Let us strong-name the assembly, and nobody will be able to swap our code." Is he right?
options: No: a strong name is identity, not protection; Authenticode and NuGet package signing prove the author
Yes: the CLR checks the signature on every load
Yes, but only in .NET 8 and later
No: only Microsoft assemblies may be strong-named
cards.explain: The modern runtime does not check the strong-name signature, Framework has long skipped it during normal loading too, and the keys of many libraries are public.

cards.q: A .NET 8 app was built against Acme.Pricing with AssemblyVersion 3.7.0.0. Deployment put the old 3.6.0.0 assembly into the folder. What happens?
options: FileLoadException: the version found is lower than requested
It loads: only the major version is checked
It loads: .NET 8 does not check versions
MissingMethodException at process start
cards.explain: "No lower" cuts both ways: higher is fine, lower is a load error. MissingMethodException would happen if both had AssemblyVersion 3.0.0.0 and the check passed.

units.blurb: How dotnet app.dll reaches Main: apphost, hostfxr, hostpolicy and picking a version with rollForward. AssemblyLoadContext instead of AppDomain — plugins, isolation and unloading, plus why the process crashes and what single-file and trimming change.

lessons.title: The host chain
lessons.sub: Muxer, apphost, hostfxr, hostpolicy and coreclr

cards.title: Five native libraries before Main
cards.body:
In the first unit the startup chain was a five-step diagram. Now let us open each step. Before your Main runs, only native C++ programs are at work; there is no managed code yet:

  • dotnet (the muxer) or app.exe (the apphost) is the entry point;
  • hostfxr picks the runtime version;
  • hostpolicy builds the list of assemblies;
  • coreclr is the runtime itself: GC, JIT, type loader.

Each part has its own folder in the .NET install, and their versions do not have to match.
cards.code:
/usr/share/dotnet/
    dotnet                                  # muxer
    host/fxr/8.0.17/libhostfxr.so
    host/fxr/9.0.6/libhostfxr.so
    shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App/8.0.17/    # libhostpolicy, libcoreclr, System.*.dll
    shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App/9.0.6/
    shared/Microsoft.AspNetCore.App/9.0.6/
    sdk/9.0.301/

cards.title: The muxer: one dotnet for every version
cards.body:
The dotnet command is the muxer (short for multiplexer). There is one per install, and it looks at the arguments: dotnet app.dll means run an app, dotnet build means an SDK command.

The muxer itself does almost nothing. It takes hostfxr from the host/fxr/<newest version> folder next to it and hands over all the work. A newer hostfxr can start older runtimes too, so the freshest one is enough.

The runtime version for the app is chosen later, inside hostfxr, and it does not depend on the version of hostfxr.
cards.deep:
For SDK commands hostfxr looks for global.json, walking up from the current folder, and picks an SDK from the sdk/ folder. global.json is not read when running an app: it configures the tools, not the runtime.

dotnet --list-runtimes, dotnet --list-sdks and dotnet --info show what is installed. The last one also prints the version of the host itself.

cards.q: Runtimes 8.0.17 and 9.0.6 are installed, and host/fxr has folders 8.0.17 and 9.0.6. You run dotnet app.dll, and the app targets net8.0. Whose hostfxr gets loaded?
options: From host/fxr/9.0.6
From host/fxr/8.0.17
From the folder next to app.dll
From shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App/8.0.17
cards.explain: The muxer always takes the newest hostfxr from host/fxr. That hostfxr then reads runtimeconfig.json and picks runtime 8.0.17 for the app.

wrong.1: The muxer does not yet know which version the app targets: hostfxr finds that out. So the newest one is taken.
wrong.3: The framework folder holds hostpolicy and coreclr. hostfxr lives separately, in host/fxr.

cards.title: The apphost: app.exe is not your program
cards.body:
Next to app.dll the build puts app.exe (just app on Linux). This is the apphost, a small native launcher from the SDK. During the build the SDK copies the template and writes the name app.dll into it. None of your code is inside.

The apphost has one job: find hostfxr. For a framework-dependent app it searches for a .NET install in order and takes the first one found:

  • the folder in DOTNET_ROOT (there are per-architecture variants such as DOTNET_ROOT_X64);
  • the registered location: on Windows the registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\dotnet\Setup\InstalledVersions\<arch>, on Linux and macOS the file /etc/dotnet/install_location;
  • the default location: %ProgramFiles%\dotnet, /usr/share/dotnet, /usr/local/share/dotnet.

The PATH variable plays no part in this search.
cards.deep:
The apphost template contains a placeholder: the SHA-256 of the string "foobar" written as text, 64 hex characters at the start of a 1024-byte buffer. The SDK finds that string and writes the dll path over it. That is why you cannot rename app.dll after the build: the apphost will look for the old name.

Since .NET 9 you can set the search order at build time with the AppHostDotNetSearch property (AppLocal, AppRelative, EnvironmentVariable, Global) and AppHostRelativeDotNet. UseAppHost=false turns the apphost off. Microsoft recommends launching through the apphost: the process list shows the app name instead of dotnet, and you can attach a manifest and an icon to the exe.

cards.q: app.exe is built as framework-dependent. Where does it look for a .NET install? Select all.
options: In the folder from DOTNET_ROOT
In the registered install location
In the default install location
In every folder on PATH
In the SDK folder named in global.json
cards.explain: The order is DOTNET_ROOT, then the registered location, then the default path. The first install found wins. PATH helps the shell find the dotnet command, but the apphost does not read it. global.json only concerns the SDK.

cards.title: hostfxr: which frameworks are needed
cards.body:
hostfxr reads app.runtimeconfig.json. It records which shared frameworks the app needs and their minimum version: always Microsoft.NETCore.App, plus Microsoft.AspNetCore.App for a web app and Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App for WPF and WinForms.

Frameworks are layered: ASP.NET Core has its own runtimeconfig that refers to NETCore.App. hostfxr resolves the whole chain, picks suitable installed versions by the roll-forward rules (the next lesson covers them) and loads hostpolicy from the folder of the chosen Microsoft.NETCore.App.

If no suitable version is found, startup ends here with "You must install or update .NET" and a list of what was found.
cards.deep: A self-contained app has includedFrameworks in runtimeconfig.json instead of frameworks: the runtime sits right next to it and hostfxr searches for nothing. The same hostfxr is the entry point for native programs that want to run .NET inside themselves: the hostfxr_initialize_for_runtime_config function, and the nethost library (get_hostfxr_path) helps find hostfxr itself.

cards.q: Put the startup steps of app.exe (framework-dependent) in order
items: The apphost finds a .NET install and loads hostfxr
hostfxr reads app.runtimeconfig.json and picks a framework version
hostfxr loads hostpolicy from that framework folder
hostpolicy reads deps.json and builds the assembly list
hostpolicy loads coreclr and passes the list to it
The CLR loads System.Private.CoreLib and calls Main
cards.explain: Each layer knows only its own file: hostfxr knows runtimeconfig.json, hostpolicy knows deps.json. Managed code appears only at the last step.

cards.title: hostpolicy: the assembly list before startup
cards.body:
hostpolicy reads app.deps.json and the deps.json of each framework (what they contain is covered in the unit "Assemblies and versions") and turns them into full paths to files. The main result is the TPA (Trusted Platform Assemblies), the very list of every app and framework assembly from the unit "Assemblies and versions". Now you can see who builds it and when.

hostpolicy passes this list and the native library paths to coreclr_initialize as properties, then calls coreclr_execute_assembly.

Hence the main difference from .NET Framework: the CLR does not walk the disk looking for an assembly. The default context takes the path from the TPA by simple name. Not in the list means not found, even if the file sits right next to the app.
cards.code:
// simplified: what hostpolicy passes to the runtime
coreclr_initialize(exePath, ..., properties)
    TRUSTED_PLATFORM_ASSEMBLIES   = .../System.Runtime.dll : /app/app.dll : /app/Dapper.dll
    NATIVE_DLL_SEARCH_DIRECTORIES = /app/ : /usr/share/dotnet/shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App/8.0.17/
    APP_CONTEXT_BASE_DIRECTORY    = /app/
coreclr_execute_assembly(..., "/app/app.dll", ...)
cards.deep:
All these properties are visible from code: AppContext.GetData("TRUSTED_PLATFORM_ASSEMBLIES"), and the list of deps.json files read is AppContext.GetData("APP_CONTEXT_DEPS_FILES"). The path separator is ";" on Windows and ":" elsewhere.

If there is no deps.json at all, hostpolicy assumes every dependency is in the app folder and builds the TPA from its contents. The DOTNET_ADDITIONAL_DEPS variable adds more deps files, but only for framework-dependent apps.

cards.q: You copied Extra.dll into the app folder by hand. The code references it statically, but app.deps.json does not list it. What happens the first time a type from Extra is used?
options: FileNotFoundException: the assembly is not in the TPA
The assembly loads from the app folder
An error at startup, before Main
hostpolicy adds it to deps.json
cards.explain: When deps.json exists, the TPA is built from it alone. The default context looks the assembly up by name in that list and does not search the folder. Fix it in the project (a package or assembly reference) or with a fresh publish, not by copying files.

wrong.1: That is how .NET Framework behaved: it probed the app folder. Modern .NET reads the folder only when there is no deps.json at all.
wrong.2: hostpolicy does not check what the code references. Assemblies load lazily, on first use.

cards.title: coreclr: one runtime per process
cards.body:
coreclr starts the garbage collector, loads the JIT (clrjit), reads System.Private.CoreLib, creates the single AppDomain and the default load context, and calls Main.

An important limit: a process can run only one runtime. You cannot keep .NET 8 and .NET 9 side by side. A native program that runs .NET inside itself (an editor plugin, a COM server) gets the already loaded runtime if it fits, or an error.
cards.deep: Besides the muxer and the apphost, .NET has other native hosts: comhost (a managed COM server), ijwhost (C++/CLI assemblies), nethost (for arbitrary native programs). All of them lead to the same hostfxr. Native AOT has no such chain at all: the runtime is compiled into the executable itself.

cards.q: Match each component with its job
pairs: Decides: run an app or an SDK command
Finds a .NET install for one app
Picks the framework version from runtimeconfig.json
GC, JIT and the type loader

cards.title: When it will not start: host tracing
cards.body: Failures before Main show up neither in the app logs nor in a managed debugger. Turn on host tracing: each layer writes what it looked for, where, and what it picked.
cards.code:
# Linux, macOS
COREHOST_TRACE=1 COREHOST_TRACEFILE=host.txt ./app

# what is installed
dotnet --list-runtimes
cards.deep: COREHOST_TRACE_VERBOSITY sets the detail level from 1 to 4. Newer hosts also accept the names DOTNET_HOST_TRACE, DOTNET_HOST_TRACEFILE and DOTNET_HOST_TRACE_VERBOSITY, but the .NET 9 host and older ones do not understand them, while the COREHOST_* names work everywhere. The trace shows which hostfxr was loaded, which runtimeconfig.json was read, which framework versions were considered, and the full TPA.

cards.q: An app is published self-contained. The server has DOTNET_ROOT pointing at an installed .NET 9. Which runtime starts?
options: The one in the app folder
The one in DOTNET_ROOT, the variable wins
The newest one installed globally
Startup fails: two runtimes conflict
cards.explain: The apphost of a self-contained app finds hostfxr next to itself, and runtimeconfig.json lists includedFrameworks. Global installs and DOTNET_ROOT are not used in this mode.

lessons.title: Which runtime starts
lessons.sub: runtimeconfig.json, rollForward and publishing modes

cards.title: runtimeconfig.json: a minimum version
cards.body:
The build writes app.runtimeconfig.json from the project TargetFramework. The key data in it is the framework name and version. This is the minimum version, not the one you built against: for net8.0 it says 8.0.0.

configProperties receives runtime settings from the project: GC mode, invariant globalization and others. The runtime reads them at startup, and code sees them through AppContext. You can edit them right in the file on the server, without rebuilding.
cards.deep: A web app has a frameworks array instead of framework, for example Microsoft.AspNetCore.App; NETCore.App comes in through the runtimeconfig of ASP.NET Core itself. The RuntimeFrameworkVersion project property raises the minimum version for a framework-dependent app, and for a self-contained one it sets the exact version that ships with it.

cards.title: rollForward: six policies
cards.body:
How to pick an installed version when 8.0.0 is requested is decided by the rollForward policy. The patch version is almost always the latest: that is how an app gets security fixes without a rebuild.

  • Minor (the default): the same major and minor, latest patch. If that minor is missing, the nearest higher minor. It never moves to another major version.
  • Major: like Minor, but if the requested major is missing entirely, it takes the nearest higher major, at its lowest minor.
  • LatestPatch: latest patch only, minor roll-forward is disabled.
  • LatestMinor: the highest minor of the same major, even if the requested one is present.
  • LatestMajor: the highest version of all, even if the requested one is present.
  • Disable: exactly the specified version, no patches. For testing only.
cards.deep:
Since .NET 5 there have been no minor releases: every version is X.0.patch. So in practice Minor means "latest patch of your own major", and the real choice is between Minor, Major and LatestMajor.

Prerelease versions (preview, rc) are not picked by default when a release version is requested. The DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD_TO_PRERELEASE=1 variable changes that.

cards.q: An app targets net8.0 and rollForward is not set. The machine has only runtimes 9.0.6 and 10.0.0 installed. What happens?
options: It does not start: "You must install or update .NET"
It runs on 9.0.6
It runs on 10.0.0
It runs on 9.0.6 with a console warning
cards.explain: The default is Minor, and it never moves to another major version. To run on 9, set rollForward to Major: in the project, with the DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD variable or with the --roll-forward option.

wrong.1: That is what the Major policy would do. Minor, the default, does not move to another major version.
wrong.2: LatestMajor would pick the newest one.

cards.q: Match each policy with its behavior
pairs: Next major, only if its own is missing
Newest installed, even if its own is present

cards.q: An app requests 8.0.0 with rollForward = Major. Installed: 8.2.3, 8.4.5, 9.0.6 and 9.7.8 (an example with minor versions, so the rule is visible). What does hostfxr pick?
cards.explain: Major version 8 is present, so Major behaves like Minor: 8.0 is missing, so the nearest higher minor, 8.2, at its latest patch, 8.2.3. This example comes from the Microsoft documentation.

wrong.1: Major moves to the next major only when its own major is missing entirely. And 8.x is installed.
wrong.2: LatestMajor would take the newest one.
wrong.3: LatestMinor would take the highest minor. Minor and Major take the nearest one.

cards.title: Where to set it and who wins
cards.body:
The policy can be set in four places. The <RollForward> project property is simply written into runtimeconfig.json. At startup the order is as follows, each one overriding the previous:

  • rollForward in runtimeconfig.json;
  • the DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD environment variable;
  • the --roll-forward option at launch.

The "version 2" scenario: you shipped a tool for .NET 8 with Major so it runs where only .NET 10 is installed. Convenient, but the app will run on a runtime you never tested it on. Microsoft publishes behavior changes between major versions as breaking changes.
cards.code:
dotnet app.dll --roll-forward Major
DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD=LatestMajor ./app

<RollForward>Major</RollForward>   <!-- in .csproj -->

cards.q: A net8.0 app should run on .NET 8 when it is present, and otherwise on the nearest newer major version. Complete the project.
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <TargetFramework>net8.0</TargetFramework>
  <RollForward>___</RollForward>
</PropertyGroup>
cards.explain: Major sticks to its own major version while it is present and moves to the next one only when it is missing. LatestMajor would go to the newest one even with .NET 8 installed.

cards.title: Self-contained: the runtime travels with the app
cards.body:
A framework-dependent app is small and uses the machine-wide .NET. When an admin installs a patch, the app gets it on its next start.

A self-contained app carries the runtime with it: hostfxr, hostpolicy, coreclr and the libraries sit in the app folder. It is published for a specific platform (a RID such as linux-x64) and weighs tens of megabytes.

The price: the runtime version is chosen at publish time, the latest patch the SDK knows about. There is no roll-forward. When a security fix comes out, you must rebuild and redeploy the app.
cards.code: dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained true

cards.q: What is true for a self-contained app? Select all.
options: The machine needs no installed .NET
Security patches arrive when a new .NET is installed on the machine
It is published for a specific RID
The rollForward policy has no effect on runtime choice
The same output runs on both Windows and Linux
cards.explain: The runtime sits in the app folder, and a global install is neither needed nor used. Hence the downside: the runtime can be updated only by a new publish. The native parts of the runtime differ per OS, so publishing targets a RID.

cards.title: Single-file: assemblies without files
cards.body:
PublishSingleFile=true appends a bundle to the apphost: the managed assemblies, runtimeconfig.json and deps.json. It works for both self-contained and framework-dependent apps.

At startup the managed assemblies are not extracted to disk: the runtime reads them straight from the bundle, in memory. Native libraries may stay as separate files next to it. The IncludeNativeLibrariesForSelfExtract property puts them inside too, but then they are extracted to a temp folder at startup.

The consequence for code: an assembly no longer has a path on disk. Assembly.Location returns an empty string, and Assembly.CodeBase throws. For files next to the program use AppContext.BaseDirectory.
cards.deep: The extraction folder is set by DOTNET_BUNDLE_EXTRACT_BASE_DIR; without it, it is $HOME/.net on Linux and macOS and %TEMP%\.net on Windows. Under systemd $HOME may be unset, so set the variable explicitly. The single-file analyzer flags risky calls with IL3000 and related codes. Environment.ProcessPath (since .NET 6) gives the path to the exe itself.

cards.q: The app is published with PublishSingleFile=true. Which line does not give the path you need?
cards.explain: The assembly was loaded from the bundle, it has no file, and Location is an empty string. ProcessPath and BaseDirectory work: the first points at the exe itself, the second at its folder.

cards.title: Trimming: what is removed cannot be loaded
cards.body:
PublishTrimmed=true turns on ILLink: it walks static references from the entry point and removes from the app and the framework libraries everything it did not reach. It works only for self-contained apps: the machine-wide shared runtime cannot be trimmed.

What breaks is anything the code finds at run time: reflection by string names, Assembly.LoadFrom with plugins, Reflection.Emit. The analyzer flags such places with IL2xxx warnings, and the [RequiresUnreferencedCode] and [DynamicallyAccessedMembers] attributes help it understand the code.

For loading this means: a separately built plugin may call a framework method that was removed, and get a MissingMethodException.
cards.deep:
TrimMode sets the scope: full trims all assemblies, partial only those marked IsTrimmable. Feature switches such as EventSourceSupport=false or InvariantGlobalization=true do two things: they let ILLink remove code, and they write the value into runtimeconfig.json so the runtime does not take the removed path.

Trimming turns off incompatible features: built-in COM interop and DOTNET_STARTUP_HOOKS startup hooks. The SDK does not support trimming for WPF and WinForms. Native AOT always trims; the lesson on ahead-of-time compilation in the first unit covers it.

cards.q: A plugin host is published with PublishTrimmed=true. Plugins are compiled separately and loaded from a folder. What is the risk?
options: A plugin may call a framework API that is gone after trimming
None: ILLink sees the plugins folder at publish time
Plugins will not load: a trimmed app has no AssemblyLoadContext
Plugins get trimmed on first load
cards.explain: ILLink kept only what the host itself needs. It never saw the plugin, so methods needed only by the plugin may have been removed. This is a known incompatibility: plugin systems and trimming do not get along.

wrong.2: Assembly loading works; the analyzer just warns about it. The problem is missing code inside the framework.
wrong.3: Trimming happens once, at publish time. Nothing is trimmed at run time.

lessons.title: AssemblyLoadContext and plugins
lessons.sub: AppDomain then, load contexts now

cards.title: Then: AppDomain, a process inside a process
cards.body:
In .NET Framework one process could hold several application domains (AppDomains). Each had its own loaded assemblies and its own static fields. A call into another domain went through remoting: the object was either serialized or derived from MarshalByRefObject and called through a proxy. It was slow.

In return, AppDomain.Unload unloaded a whole domain, by force: its threads were aborted and its assemblies vanished. That is how IIS kept several sites in one process and restarted them one at a time.

Now: .NET (Core) has one domain. AppDomain.CurrentDomain stays for its events, UnhandledException, ProcessExit, AssemblyResolve, but you cannot create a new domain.
cards.deep: Why it was dropped: domain isolation was expensive to implement and was not a real security boundary, since fully trusted code could escape the domain. Microsoft porting advice: for isolation use a separate process or container; for loading and unloading code use AssemblyLoadContext. Remoting and the Code Access Security sandbox went away together with domains.

cards.q: Old plugin host code is being ported to .NET 8. What does this line do?
cards.code: AppDomain sandbox = AppDomain.CreateDomain("plugins");
options: Throws PlatformNotSupportedException at run time
Does not compile: the method is gone
Creates a new domain, as in .NET Framework
Returns the current domain
cards.explain: The method is kept in the API for source compatibility, so the code compiles. But when called it throws PlatformNotSupportedException: modern .NET cannot create a second domain.

wrong.1: The AppDomain class and the CreateDomain method are in the API; otherwise porting old code would break at build time.

cards.title: Now: AssemblyLoadContext
cards.body:
An AssemblyLoadContext (ALC) is a dictionary "simple assembly name to loaded assembly" plus rules for where to find missing ones. The key rule: within one context a name has one version. If the assembly is already loaded, a request for another version succeeds only if the loaded one is not lower than the requested one.

AssemblyLoadContext.Default is created at startup and loads from the TPA, the list hostpolicy built. It cannot be unloaded, and its lookup can be customized only through events.

Your own context is a new dictionary. In it you can load Newtonsoft.Json 12 while the host works with version 13.
cards.deep: The isolation here is by name only: contexts share one heap, one GC, the same threads. A type loaded into two contexts is two different types with their own static fields and their own MethodTables. To find an assembly context use AssemblyLoadContext.GetLoadContext(assembly); all contexts in the process: AssemblyLoadContext.All.

cards.q: What does a separate AssemblyLoadContext give you? Select all.
options: Two versions of one library in one process
Separate static fields for a copy of a type loaded into this context
Memory protection: a plugin cannot corrupt host objects
Assembly unloading, if the context is created collectible
A separate heap and its own garbage collector
cards.explain: A context isolates names, not memory. The heap, the GC and the threads are shared, and plugin code can do anything to host objects that its references allow. For real isolation run the plugin in a separate process.

cards.title: How a context finds an assembly by name
cards.body:
First the active context is chosen. For a static reference it is the context that loaded the referring assembly. That is why plugin dependencies go into the plugin context by themselves.

Then the active context tries in order and stops at the first success:

  • its own cache by name;
  • its own Load method, the one you override;
  • the default context: its cache and the TPA;
  • the Resolving event of the active context;
  • the AppDomain.AssemblyResolve event.

A Load that returns null means "not mine, ask Default". Splitting off shared assemblies is built on this.

cards.q: A plugin first touches a type from Dapper. Put in order where the plugin context looks for the assembly
items: The plugin context cache by name
The overridden Load of the plugin context
Default: its cache and the TPA
The Resolving event of the plugin context
The AppDomain.AssemblyResolve event
cards.explain: Own cache, own Load, then Default, and only then the events. The AssemblyResolve handler is the last chance, shared by the whole process.

cards.title: One type, two identities
cards.body:
A type in .NET is defined not just by its name but by the assembly instance. If the plugin context loads its own copy of Contracts.dll, the host IPlugin and the plugin IPlugin are different types. A cast in the host throws InvalidCastException, and the message names both types identically.

The rule: shared contracts live only in Default. The plugin Load returns null for them, and they are not put into the plugin folder at all:
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <EnableDynamicLoading>true</EnableDynamicLoading>
</PropertyGroup>
<ItemGroup>
  <ProjectReference Include="..\Contracts\Contracts.csproj">
    <Private>false</Private>
    <ExcludeAssets>runtime</ExcludeAssets>
  </ProjectReference>
</ItemGroup>
cards.deep:
EnableDynamicLoading marks the project as a dynamically loaded component: all dependencies are copied to the output, and plugin.deps.json appears. Private=false and ExcludeAssets=runtime keep Contracts.dll (and its package dependencies) out of the plugin folder.

To find where two "identical" types came from, compare a.GetType().Assembly and AssemblyLoadContext.GetLoadContext(...) for both objects.

cards.q: The host loads a plugin into its own context. The line (IPlugin)Activator.CreateInstance(type)! throws InvalidCastException, although the type implements IPlugin. The plugin folder contains Contracts.dll. What is the cause?
options: The plugin context loaded its own copy of Contracts.dll
The plugin targets a different .NET version
Activator cannot create types from another context
IPlugin must be marked [Serializable]
cards.explain: The plugin Load found Contracts.dll next to it and loaded it into the plugin context. Now that context has its own IPlugin. Remove the contracts assembly from the plugin output or return null for it in Load; then it comes from Default, shared with the host.

wrong.3: [Serializable] and marshaling were needed for calls between domains. Contexts share one heap, and the object is passed by reference.

cards.title: AssemblyDependencyResolver: the plugin deps.json
cards.body: Where the plugin dependencies are is recorded in its plugin.deps.json (the format is in the unit "Assemblies and versions"). AssemblyDependencyResolver reads it and turns the name of an assembly or a native library into a full path. Found: load it into the plugin context. Not found (a framework assembly or a shared contract): null, and the assembly comes from Default.
cards.deep: The resolver understands the same things as hostpolicy: runtimes/<rid>/ folders for platform-specific assemblies, native libraries, satellite resource assemblies. So a plugin with a native dependency (SQLite, for example) works without hand-parsing folders. If an assembly exists in both the host and the plugin, Load makes the choice: return a path and the plugin gets its own copy, return null and it gets the shared one from Default.

cards.q: Complete the Load method of the plugin context
cards.explain: LoadFromAssemblyPath is a method of this same context, so the assembly lands in it. Assembly.LoadFrom would load it into Default, and the isolation would be gone.

cards.title: LoadFrom, LoadFile and Load(byte[]) today
cards.body:
The old Assembly methods still work, but on top of contexts:

  • Assembly.LoadFrom(path) loads into Default and adds an AssemblyResolve handler that looks for dependencies in the same folder;
  • Assembly.LoadFile(path) loads into a new unnamed context;
  • Assembly.Load(byte[]) also loads into a new context, one per call.

The Default trap: if an assembly with that name is in the TPA, the default context takes it, even if you explicitly passed another path or stream. That is why plugins are loaded into their own context, not into Default.
cards.deep: Assembly.LoadFile caches assemblies by path: a second call with the same path returns the same assembly. The dependencies of such an assembly are found by the normal algorithm, which mostly means Default. Assembly.Load(string) and Type.GetType(string) pick the active context from the calling code or from AssemblyLoadContext.CurrentContextualReflectionContext; EnterContextualReflection sets it so that reflection inside a plugin finds plugin assemblies.

cards.q: The host TPA contains Newtonsoft.Json 13. The host calls AssemblyLoadContext.Default.LoadFromAssemblyPath("plugins/Newtonsoft.Json.dll"), which is version 12. What gets loaded?
options: Version 13 from the TPA
Version 12 from the plugins folder
Both: Default will hold two versions
FileLoadException: version conflict
cards.explain: In the default context an assembly in the TPA with the same name takes precedence over the given path. To get version 12 you must load it into a separate context.

wrong.2: Within one context a name has only one version. Two versions are possible only in two contexts.

cards.q: Where does the assembly go?
pairs: A static reference from a plugin assembly
The plugin context starts the lookup
Into Default, dependencies from the same folder

lessons.title: Unloading and crashes
lessons.sub: Collectible contexts, what keeps them alive, and unhandled exceptions

cards.title: Collectible: a context you can unload
cards.body:
A context created with isCollectible: true can be unloaded together with all its assemblies (since .NET Core 3.0). The plugin code, its types and the machine code the JIT produced live in that context memory and are freed with it.

But unloading is cooperative. Unload() only starts it. The garbage collector finishes it, once no strong references from outside point at the context assemblies, types and objects, and no thread is running its code.

This is the opposite of AppDomain.Unload, which aborted threads by force. Here nobody aborts anything: whatever holds the context keeps it.
cards.deep: Inside the runtime the context memory belongs to a LoaderAllocator object. While it is reachable, nothing is freed. Limitations: C++/CLI assemblies cannot be loaded into a collectible context, and ReadyToRun machine code in such assemblies is ignored, so the JIT compiles the methods.

cards.q: The alc.Unload() call has returned. Are the plugin assemblies unloaded already?
options: No: unloading has only started, the GC finishes it once no references remain
Yes, right after Unload returns
Yes, and the plugin threads are aborted, as with AppDomain
No: a collectible context unloads only at process exit
cards.explain: Unload puts the context into the unloading state. Only the garbage collector can free the memory, and it does so when the context becomes unreachable.

wrong.2: AppDomain unloaded by force. AssemblyLoadContext aborts nobody: a thread running plugin code keeps the context alive.

cards.title: What keeps a context alive
cards.body:
Unloading is blocked by any strong reference from outside to an assembly, type or object of the context, and by context code on the stack of any thread. In practice:

  • host static fields and caches: a Type → handler dictionary, the last plugin result;
  • subscriptions: the plugin subscribed to a host event, so the event delegate references the plugin object;
  • plugin threads and timers: a thread in Thread.Sleep, a Timer, a RegisteredWaitHandle with a plugin callback;
  • strong GCHandles, normal and pinned;
  • local variables, including invisible temporaries the JIT introduced;
  • fields of your AssemblyLoadContext subclass that reference plugin assemblies and objects.

A WeakReference does not block unloading.
cards.deep: The last item is sneaky: while unloading is in progress, the runtime itself holds a strong handle to the context object. So subclass fields pointing at an Assembly or plugin objects will not be collected even after you let go of the context. Clear them. The AssemblyLoadContext.Unloading event is where a plugin can stop its threads and free its GCHandles.

cards.q: What will prevent the plugin context from unloading? Select all.
options: A host static field holds a plugin object
The plugin subscribed to a static host event
A plugin background thread sleeps in Thread.Sleep
The host keeps a WeakReference to the context
The plugin passed a string to the host, and the host stored it
cards.explain: A static field and a delegate in an event are strong references to a plugin object. A sleeping thread keeps plugin code on its stack. A WeakReference does not count. A string is a System.String from CoreLib, not a plugin type: it does not hold the context.

cards.title: How to unload and make sure
cards.body:
Everything that touches the plugin goes into a separate method marked NoInlining: otherwise the JIT may inline it into the caller, and references to the context stay in the caller stack. Only a WeakReference is handed out.

Then you run garbage collection while the reference is alive. One pass is usually enough. If plugin objects have finalizers, it takes several: a finalizer keeps its object alive for one more collection.
cards.deep: If the context does not unload, take a dump and find what holds it. In WinDbg or LLDB with the SOS extension, dumpheap -type LoaderAllocator shows the context object and gcroot <address> shows the reference chain to a root. The root can be a stack slot, a static field or a GCHandle. If a thread running plugin code holds the context, the thread stacks show it (clrstack).

cards.q: After RunPlugin and the GC.Collect loop the context is still alive. Registry is a static host class. Which line blocks unloading?
cards.explain: A host static field is a GC root. Through the plugin object it holds its type, its assembly and the whole context. The method locals disappear after it returns; the static field does not.

cards.title: An unhandled exception: the process goes down
cards.body:
An exception nobody catches terminates the whole process, whatever thread it happens on: the main thread, a new Thread, the thread pool, the finalizer thread.

Then: in .NET Framework 1.x exceptions on pool threads and the finalizer were silently swallowed, and only the thread died. Version 2.0 made the policy strict, and the legacyUnhandledExceptionPolicy flag in app.config brought the old behavior back. Modern .NET has no such flag.

Why: a thread that dies quietly leaves program state half-changed, and the program goes on with corrupted data. Better to fail at once and loudly.
cards.deep: The runtime itself swallows only the service exceptions it uses to control threads: in Framework, ThreadAbortException and AppDomainUnloadedException on threads the CLR created. In .NET 5+ Thread.Abort throws PlatformNotSupportedException. A stack overflow cannot be caught at all: the process ends without events or finally blocks; the stack lesson in the memory course covers it.

cards.q: The host calls plugin.Run() inside try/catch (Exception). Inside Run the plugin does new Thread(() => throw new InvalidOperationException()).Start() and returns at once. What happens?
options: The process terminates: nobody caught the exception on the other thread
The host catch catches the exception
Only the plugin thread dies, the host keeps running
The plugin context unloads automatically
cards.explain: try/catch catches only exceptions of its own thread. The new thread has no handler, so the exception becomes unhandled, and that terminates the whole process. An assembly load context does not protect against crashes.

wrong.2: That was .NET Framework 1.x. Since 2.0 an unhandled exception on any thread terminates the process.

cards.title: UnhandledException is a notice, not a rescue
cards.body:
The AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException event arrives before termination. In it you can write a log, flush buffers, save a dump. You cannot cancel the crash: e.IsTerminating is true.

What does not bring the process down:

  • an exception in a Task nobody awaited: since .NET 4.5 it only raises TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException when the GC collects the task;
  • an exception caught in a catch.

But async void does crash it: the exception has nowhere to return, so it is thrown on the synchronization context or the thread pool.
cards.deep:
.NET 10 added ExceptionHandling.SetUnhandledExceptionHandler(Func<Exception, bool>) in System.Runtime.ExceptionServices. The documentation names its purpose: hosts such as REPLs and game scripting that cannot otherwise handle exceptions thrown by plugins. The handler returns true if the exception was handled, and it can be set once; a second call throws InvalidOperationException. Check the documentation for your version on which threads and cases it covers before building a host on it.

In .NET Framework a native host could change the policy through ICLRPolicyManager::SetUnhandledExceptionPolicy.

cards.q: What terminates the process by default in .NET 8? Select all.
options: An exception in a method started with new Thread
An exception in an async void method
An exception in a Task nobody awaited
An exception in a ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem callback
An exception caught in catch and logged
cards.explain: A thread, async void and a pool callback have no handler above them, so the exception becomes unhandled. A task nobody awaited only raises UnobservedTaskException during garbage collection.

cards.title: Summary: what a plugin context protects against
cards.body:
It protects against dependency version conflicts, and it lets you unload a plugin and load a new version without a restart.

It does not protect against crashes, since an exception on a plugin thread terminates the host; against memory corruption and infinite loops, since the heap and the CPU are shared; against leaks, since a forgotten subscription holds the whole context.

A plugin you do not trust, or one that crashes often, needs a separate process: you can kill it, restart it and cap its memory with OS tools. That is what replaces what domains used to do.

cards.q: The host subscribed to UnhandledException and writes a log in the handler. A plugin timer throws an exception in its callback. What happens?
options: The log is written, then the process terminates
The log is written, and the host keeps running
The handler is not called: the exception is from another context
The timer stops, everything else keeps running
cards.explain: A timer callback runs on the thread pool, and an exception in it becomes unhandled. The UnhandledException event is process-wide: it arrives, but it cannot cancel termination.

wrong.2: Load contexts do not split the process into domains. There is one UnhandledException event for the whole process.

lessons.title: Final: loading and hosting
lessons.sub: The host, runtime versions, contexts, unloading and crashes

cards.q: Assemble the startup of dotnet app.dll from the command to Main
items: The muxer takes the newest hostfxr from host/fxr
hostfxr reads runtimeconfig.json and picks a Microsoft.NETCore.App version
hostpolicy from the framework folder builds the TPA from deps.json
coreclr starts the GC and JIT and loads System.Private.CoreLib
The default context loads app.dll, and Main is called
cards.explain: hostfxr picks the runtime version, not the muxer. The assembly list is ready before the CLR starts, and the default context takes assemblies from it.

cards.q: An app requests 8.0.0. Installed: 8.0.17, 9.0.6 and 10.0.2. runtimeconfig.json says rollForward = Major, but the service is started with DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD=LatestMajor. Which runtime is picked?
options: Startup fails: the settings contradict each other
cards.explain: The environment variable overrides runtimeconfig.json, and LatestMajor takes the newest version even when its own major is present. With Major from the file, 8.0.17 would be picked.

wrong.1: That is what Major from runtimeconfig.json would decide. But DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD outranks the file.
wrong.2: Major would take the nearest next major, and only if 8.x were missing entirely.

cards.q: What is true about hosting? Select all.
options: DOTNET_ROOT overrides the registered install location for the apphost
global.json affects the runtime choice for dotnet app.dll
One process can hold both .NET 8 and .NET 9
A self-contained app has hostfxr in the app folder
cards.explain: The apphost checks DOTNET_ROOT before the registry or /etc/dotnet and takes the first install found. global.json selects only the SDK. A process always has exactly one runtime.

cards.q: The host TPA has Newtonsoft.Json 13. A plugin loads into a PluginLoadContext with an AssemblyDependencyResolver, and its folder and plugin.deps.json have Newtonsoft.Json 12. Which version does the plugin code get?
options: 12: the plugin Load found it before Default was reached
13: an assembly from the TPA always wins
Both: each call gets its own
FileLoadException: two versions of one name in the process
cards.explain: The active context for plugin references is the plugin own context. First its cache, then its Load: the resolver returned the path to version 12, and it was loaded into the plugin context. Default and the TPA were never reached.

wrong.1: The TPA beats a path only inside the default context. In your own context its Load decides.
wrong.3: Two versions in a process are fine if they are in different contexts. That is exactly what contexts are for.

cards.q: Create is a host method that loads the plugin into alc. After Run and the GC.Collect loop the context is alive. Which line blocks unloading?
cards.explain: The event of a long-lived host object stores a delegate, and the delegate references the plugin object. Through it the type, the assembly and the context are kept alive. The report string is a plain System.String and does not hold the context.

cards.q: A .NET 8 service crashed overnight. The UnhandledException handler logged an exception from a System.Threading.Timer callback. How do you keep such errors from bringing the service down?
options: Catch exceptions inside the timer callback
Set e.IsTerminating = false in the UnhandledException handler
Turn on legacyUnhandledExceptionPolicy in runtimeconfig.json
Create the timer inside a separate AssemblyLoadContext
cards.explain: A timer callback runs on the thread pool, and there is no handler above it. The only place the exception can be handled is the callback itself: a try/catch with logging and a decision about what to do next.

wrong.1: IsTerminating only reports that the process is ending. The property cannot be changed, and the crash cannot be cancelled.
wrong.2: That flag lived in the .NET Framework app.config. Modern .NET does not have it.
wrong.3: A load context isolates assembly names, not threads or exceptions.
