cards.q: You need one executable with the runtime inside, trimmed for size. Complete the project.
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <RuntimeIdentifier>linux-x64</RuntimeIdentifier>
  <SelfContained>true</SelfContained>
  <___>true</___>
  <PublishTrimmed>true</PublishTrimmed>
</PropertyGroup>
cards.explain: PublishSingleFile appends the assemblies to the apphost as one bundle. SelfContained puts the runtime inside, and PublishTrimmed removes unused code. Remember: assemblies from the bundle have an empty Assembly.Location.

cards.q: Match the symptom with its cause
pairs: The contract is loaded into two contexts
A strong reference from the host
hostfxr found no version per rollForward

cards.q: A .NET 8 security patch is out, and the admin installed it on the server. The server runs two net8.0 apps: one framework-dependent, one self-contained. Which gets the fix after a restart?
options: Only the framework-dependent one
Only the self-contained one
Both
Neither, until they are rebuilt
cards.explain: A framework-dependent app takes the latest installed patch of its version at startup. A self-contained app carries the runtime in its own folder and is updated only by a new publish.

units.title: Generics and reflection inside out
units.blurb: How the JIT shares generic code through __Canon and dictionaries, what lies behind metadata tokens, MethodInfo and Invoke, how the dynamic call site cache works, and why source generators replace reflection.

lessons.title: How the JIT shares generic code
lessons.sub: __Canon for reference T, a copy per value type, the generic dictionary and statics per instantiation

cards.title: One body of code or many copies
cards.body:
The generics unit of the Deeper C# course gave the rule: reference T share machine code, value types get their own. Now for how it actually works.

When the JIT compiles a generic method, it first reduces the instantiation to its canonical form. Every reference type argument is replaced with the internal type System.__Canon; value types stay as they are. Code is compiled once per canonical form.

So List<string> and List<Uri> run the very same List<__Canon> code, while List<int> and List<long> each get their own.
cards.code:
var a = new List<int>();     // own code: List<int>
var b = new List<long>();    // own code: List<long>
var c = new List<string>();  // shared code: List<__Canon>
var d = new List<Uri>();     // the same shared code
cards.deep:
It already worked this way in .NET Framework 2.0, and Native AOT does the same: ahead of time it compiles one canonical version for all reference T and a separate one for every value type it finds in the program.

You can see it yourself: in .NET 7+ the environment variable DOTNET_JitDisasm="Echo" prints a method's machine code. For Echo<T> called with int and string the output has two headers: Echo[int](int):int and Echo[System.__Canon](System.__Canon):System.__Canon.

cards.q: A program uses Dictionary<string, int>, Dictionary<object, int>, Dictionary<int, string> and Dictionary<int, object>. How many machine code versions of TryGetValue will the JIT produce?
cards.explain: The canonical forms are Dictionary<__Canon, int> for the first two and Dictionary<int, __Canon> for the last two. Each reference argument is replaced on its own; value types stay.

wrong.1: Reference arguments become __Canon, so string and object in the same position give the same form.
wrong.2: The value type sits in a different position: <__Canon, int> and <int, __Canon> are two different forms.

cards.title: Why value types cannot do this
cards.body:
Every reference is 8 bytes of address (on x64), and the garbage collector walks it the same way no matter what it points to. Code that copies, stores and compares references does not care whether it holds a string or a Uri.

Value types differ in substance:

  • size: int is 4 bytes, decimal is 16, your own struct is whatever it is;
  • reference map (GC info): a struct may contain references, and the collector has to know where;
  • operations: comparing two int values is one instruction, comparing two structs is a call to their method.

Shared code for them would have to go through boxing. Instead the JIT makes a separate copy, and in that copy it can inline the methods of T and skip boxing entirely.
cards.deep:
The price of copies is code size: every value type instantiation means new methods in memory and more JIT time. That is why libraries with a huge number of structs inside generics take noticeably longer to warm up.

The canonical form is built recursively. A generic struct over reference types is canonicalized too: KeyValuePair<string, int> and KeyValuePair<object, int> both reduce to KeyValuePair<__Canon, int>, and a List of such pairs shares code in CoreCLR. But now it is a value type with shared code, so it needs the same exact-type lookup that reference types use.

cards.q: Which instantiations share the machine code of Add with List<string>? Select all.
options: List<object>
List<int[]>
List<int?>
List<DateTime>
List<Action>
cards.explain: An array and a delegate are reference types, so they also become __Canon. int? is Nullable<int>, a struct, and DateTime is a struct: each gets its own copy.

cards.title: The generic dictionary: where shared code finds T
cards.body:
Shared code does not know which T it is running for. Yet sometimes the exact type is needed: to create a T[], to check o is T, to evaluate typeof(T), to create a new List<T>(), to touch a static field.

For that every exact instantiation has a generic dictionary: a table of slots holding handles of the types and methods it needs. How shared code reaches it:

  • an instance method of a class goes through this: the object type pointer leads to its MethodTable, and the dictionary hangs off it;
  • a static method of a generic type and a method of a generic struct receive a hidden parameter from the JIT with the MethodTable of the exact type;
  • a generic method M<T> receives a hidden parameter with the handle of that particular method instantiation.
cards.deep:
The CoreCLR docs describe this in "Shared generics" (Book of the Runtime): for generic methods the hidden argument is an InstantiatedMethodDesc, for static methods and struct methods it is a MethodTable.

Slots are filled lazily. The first lookup goes into the runtime through a JIT helper function, which finds the type and writes it into the slot. After that it is a few memory loads and a null check. If the slots run out, the runtime can grow the dictionary, so the fast path may also include a size check.

Where the exact type is not needed there is no lookup: default(T) for a reference T is just null, and so are null checks, copying a T and passing it on.

cards.q: The shared code of Box<__Canon>.Check(o) executes o is T. Put the steps in order
items: Take the type pointer from this
Use the MethodTable to find this instantiation dictionary
Read the slot with the handle of T
If the slot is empty, call a runtime helper once to fill it
Compare the type of o with the T that was found
cards.explain: Box<string> and Box<Uri> run the same code, but they have different MethodTables and different dictionaries. Going through this is how the code learns which T it has right now.

cards.title: typeof(T) == typeof(int) costs nothing
cards.body:
In a copy for a value type the JIT knows T exactly. So it evaluates typeof(T) == typeof(int) at compile time and throws away the branches that can never run.

The .NET libraries build fast paths on this: the code of Span, MemoryExtensions and the numeric types is full of typeof(T) == typeof(byte) checks. The machine code for byte keeps only the right branch; for everything else, only the general one.

Shared code for reference T cannot do this: the type is found at run time through the dictionary, and the check stays a real comparison.
cards.deep: This happens in optimized code (Tier 1 and full optimization). Tier 0 compiles quickly and folds very little. Even costlier than usual are generic virtual methods (virtual void M<T>()): the exact target depends on both the object type and T, so the call goes through a runtime lookup with a cache instead of a simple method table slot. Keep them out of hot code.

cards.q: What is left in the optimized machine code of Size<long>()?
options: Only return 8
Both typeof checks and return 8
A helper call to look T up in the dictionary
Boxing T and comparing Type objects
cards.explain: long is a value type, so Size<long> has its own copy. typeof(long) == typeof(int) is known to be false, typeof(long) == typeof(long) is true. The JIT folds both checks, and all that is left of the method is returning the constant 8.

wrong.2: Only shared code needs the dictionary. In a copy for a value type T is known at compile time.

cards.title: Static fields belong to each instantiation
cards.body:
Code can be shared, data cannot. Counter<string> and Counter<object> run shared code, but they are different types: each has its own MethodTable, its own block of static fields and its own static constructor, which runs separately for every instantiation.

Shared code finds the right statics block through the generic dictionary as well: it is just another slot.
cards.deep:
This is the basis of the "static cache per type" trick: static class TypeCache<T> { public static readonly string Name = typeof(T).Name; }. The value is computed once per type, and reading it is a field load with no hashing, unlike a Dictionary<Type, …>. EqualityComparer<T>.Default and Array.Empty<T>() work this way.

A bonus: if the class is already initialized by the time a method is recompiled at Tier 1, the JIT can embed the value of a primitive static readonly field as a constant.

cards.q: Which line prints 0?
cards.explain: Registry<Uri> is a separate type with its own field, and nobody wrote to it. The fact that all three instantiations run the shared Registry<__Canon> code has no effect on statics.

cards.title: constrained.: an interface call on T without boxing
cards.body:
The method Less<T> calls CompareTo on a value of type T. If T is a struct, a plain interface call would require boxing: an interface call works on an object in the heap.

So the C# compiler puts the constrained. prefix in front of callvirt. It tells the JIT: "the call is made on a value of type T". In the copy for int the JIT calls Int32.CompareTo directly and usually inlines it: no boxing, no virtual call. In shared code for a reference T it is an ordinary interface call.
cards.deep: The prefix arrived together with generics in .NET Framework 2.0 for exactly this reason: the same IL has to work with reference T (a reference needs no boxing) and with value T (boxing must be avoided). If the struct does not override the method and it is inherited from object (for example ToString), boxing still happens, just as in the boxing lesson.

cards.q: Match each concept with what it means
pairs: Stands in for a reference T in shared code
Slots with exact types for shared code
Interface call on T without boxing
A constant in the copy for a value T

lessons.title: Reflection inside out
lessons.sub: Metadata tokens, RuntimeTypeHandle, MethodInfo caches and what Invoke really costs

cards.title: IL has no names, only tokens
cards.body:
Assembly metadata is a set of tables: types, methods, fields, references to members elsewhere. An IL instruction never contains a method name. It contains a metadata token, 4 bytes:

  • the high byte is the table number: 0x02 TypeDef, 0x06 MethodDef, 0x0A MemberRef, 0x01 TypeRef, 0x70 string literal;
  • the low three bytes are the row number in that table, starting at one.

The names shown by ildasm and ILSpy are looked up by those tools from the metadata using the token.
cards.deep:
The row numbers in the example are made up; they depend on the assembly. MethodDef is a method defined in this very assembly. MemberRef is a reference by name: a parent (a TypeRef for a foreign type, or a TypeSpec), a name and a signature blob. Calling a method on a generic instantiation such as List<int>.Add is a MemberRef whose parent is a TypeSpec (0x1B), and calling a generic method Foo<int>() uses a MethodSpec token (0x2B).

From code you can see a token as MemberInfo.MetadataToken, and Module.ResolveMethod turns it back into an object. The tables and their codes are defined in the ECMA-335 standard.

cards.q: Match the high byte of a token with its table
pairs: TypeDef: a type from this assembly
MethodDef: a method from this assembly
MemberRef: a reference to a member by name and signature
TypeRef: a reference to a type in another assembly
A string literal from the #US heap

cards.title: How the JIT turns a token into a method
cards.body:
While compiling a method, the JIT meets a call with a token and asks the runtime: what is this?

  • MethodDef is a row of its own table; the runtime finds the method descriptor (MethodDesc) right away.
  • MemberRef takes longer: follow the AssemblyRef to find and load the assembly, find the type in it by name, and find the method in the type by name and signature.

The result is remembered in the module tables, so resolution happens once. But the mechanism implies a "version 2" scenario: the signature in a MemberRef includes the parameter types and the return type. Change them in a library and a consumer built against the old version will find no match.
cards.deep:
The error does not show up when the assembly loads, but when the JIT compiles the method containing the call: MissingMethodException (or MissingFieldException for fields). So old code may run happily for a long time until it reaches the branch with the stale call.

Hence the rule for library authors: never change signatures in a public API, add an overload next to the old one. Even an optional parameter changes the signature: the default value is inserted by the calling compiler, while in metadata the method simply has one more parameter.

cards.q: In version 2 of a library, public int Count() became public long Count(). The app was not rebuilt; the new dll was dropped in. What happens?
options: MissingMethodException when the JIT compiles the calling method
It works: the long gets truncated to int
An error when the library assembly loads
The new method is called and returns a long
cards.explain: The app MemberRef records the signature "() returning int32". The new assembly has no method with that signature: the return type is part of the signature. The runtime cannot find the method when resolving the token.

wrong.2: The assembly loads fine. The error comes later, when that particular MemberRef is resolved.

cards.title: Handles are runtime pointers
cards.body:
Inside the runtime a type is a MethodTable, a method is a MethodDesc, a field is a FieldDesc. Managed code sees them through handle wrappers:

  • RuntimeTypeHandle points to a MethodTable;
  • RuntimeMethodHandle to a MethodDesc;
  • RuntimeFieldHandle to a FieldDesc.

typeof(X) compiles to ldtoken (token to handle) plus a call to Type.GetTypeFromHandle. The JIT recognizes the pair and replaces it with a constant. There is exactly one Type object (really a RuntimeType) per type: the runtime creates it the first time it is needed and hands out the same one afterwards.
cards.deep:
The check obj.GetType() == typeof(Circle) in optimized code creates no Type objects at all: the JIT compares the MethodTable pointer from the object with a constant. When you need the exact type without subclasses, this is cheaper than is Circle on an unsealed class: no walk up the hierarchy.

Since .NET 8 RuntimeType objects usually live on the non-moving NonGC heap, so the JIT can embed their address directly in machine code.

cards.q: What is true about typeof in optimized code? Select all.
options: obj.GetType() == typeof(X) becomes a comparison of MethodTable pointers
Every typeof(X) looks the type up by name in metadata
There is one RuntimeType object per type, and typeof returns that same object
typeof(X) creates a new Type object on every call
cards.explain: The token in ldtoken is resolved once, when the method is compiled; there is no lookup by name on each call. And a type has a single Type object, so typeof(X) == typeof(X) can be compared by reference.

cards.title: MethodInfo and the reflection caches
cards.body:
GetMethod("Parse") goes to the type cache (RuntimeTypeCache) that a RuntimeType creates on its first reflection request. On the first lookup the cache walks the methods of the MethodTable, creates RuntimeMethodInfo objects (each holding a RuntimeMethodHandle) and stores them.

A repeated lookup is cheaper, but not free: comparing names, filtering by BindingFlags, picking an overload by parameter types. And GetMethods() returns a fresh copy of the array every time.

The rule: look the MethodInfo up once and keep it in a static readonly field.
cards.deep:
RuntimeType holds its cache through a weak reference (a GC handle), so under memory pressure the collector may drop it and the next request rebuilds everything. That is another reason to keep the MethodInfo objects you need yourself instead of hoping a repeated GetMethod returns the same object.

Then and now: in .NET Framework this path also ran Code Access Security checks. Modern .NET has no CAS, but the visibility and argument checks on invocation are still there.

cards.q: Put in order what happens on mi.Invoke(obj, [42]) for a method void Set(int v)
items: 42 is boxed into an object and placed in an object[] array
Check: obj has a suitable type and the argument count matches
Check each argument type and unbox 42 into an int
Call the method through a stub
Return the result as object (null here)
cards.explain: One call costs an array, a boxed argument, checks and an indirect call. If the method throws, Invoke wraps the exception in TargetInvocationException.

cards.title: The cost of Invoke: then and now
cards.body:
The ways to call a method through reflection are covered in the Attributes and reflection unit of the Deeper C# course; here is what happens inside. Before .NET 7 every Invoke went down a generic path inside the runtime: parse the signature, unpack the arguments from the array, call. In .NET 7 Invoke became several times faster: after the first call the runtime generates an IL stub for the method that unpacks arguments like ordinary code.

.NET 8 added MethodInvoker and ConstructorInvoker: up to four arguments are passed without an array, and there is no Invoke-compatible handling of default values. Value type arguments are still boxed, since the parameters are object?.

The fastest option is CreateDelegate: build a delegate once, and from then on a call costs as much as a delegate call.
cards.deep:
In .NET 7+ the first call takes the old path without code generation: for a one-off call, building a stub costs more than calling slowly. Where code generation is impossible (Native AOT, RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported == false), a path without emission is used. Invoke wraps exceptions from the called method in TargetInvocationException; the BindingFlags.DoNotWrapExceptions flag turns that off.

CreateDelegate for an instance method with no target gives an "open" delegate: the object comes as the first parameter. The exact cost of each option depends on the version and the signature, so measure with BenchmarkDotNet.

cards.q: The method is known in advance, but it has to be called through reflection a million times. What do you pick?
options: CreateDelegate once, then call the delegate
MethodInfo.Invoke with a cached MethodInfo
MethodInvoker from .NET 8
dynamic: the call site cache will speed it up
cards.explain: Once created, a delegate neither checks nor boxes its arguments: it is an ordinary indirect call. Invoke and MethodInvoker pay for checks and for boxing value type arguments on every call.

wrong.2: MethodInvoker is faster than Invoke because there is no array, but value type arguments are still boxed and the checks remain.

cards.title: UnsafeAccessor inside: the runtime writes the body
cards.body:
How to use [UnsafeAccessor] (.NET 8) is covered in the Attributes and reflection unit of the Deeper C# course. Inside, it is a relative of MemberRef: you declare a static extern method with no body. When the JIT reaches it, the runtime looks the target member up by the name from the attribute and by the accessor signature, once, just like resolving a token, and generates the body itself: IL with a direct ldflda or call.

From then on it is ordinary code: it can be inlined, with no MethodInfo, no array and no boxing. And since the body is known before the app runs, Native AOT compiles it ahead of time.
cards.deep: The member is found by name and signature when the accessor method is compiled; if it is missing you get MissingFieldException or MissingMethodException. The kinds are Constructor, Method, StaticMethod, Field, StaticField. Generic support in accessors arrived in .NET 9. The price is fragility: a private member can be renamed in any release.

cards.q: Find the method once and turn it into a delegate
cards.explain: static readonly means the lookup and the delegate creation happen once, when the type is initialized. CreateDelegate<TDelegate>() gives an open delegate whose first parameter is the Calc object. Invoke would return object and pay for checks on every call.

lessons.title: dynamic and source generators
lessons.sub: CallSite<T>, the L0/L1/L2 caches, and reflection moved to compile time

cards.title: What the compiler turns dynamic into
cards.body:
The lesson "Primitives, checked and dynamic" in the Deeper C# course said: every operation on dynamic gets a call site. Now let us look at the actual code.

The compiler creates a hidden static class with a field of type CallSite<TDelegate> for each operation. On the first pass the field is filled in: CallSite.Create receives a binder, an object that describes the operation: the member name, argument flags and the type the call comes from (the binder uses it to check access to private members).

The delegate type mirrors the arguments: dynamic becomes object, while arguments with a known type keep it, so 10 goes into the call site as an int, unboxed.
cards.deep:
The real names, like <>o__0.<>p__0, are compiler details. Binder here is Microsoft.CSharp.RuntimeBinder.Binder, and argInfos is an array of CSharpArgumentInfo: for each argument, flags such as "type known at compile time", "constant", "named" and so on.

The infrastructure itself, the DLR (Dynamic Language Runtime), lives in System.Linq.Expressions and arrived in .NET Framework 4.0. IronPython and IronRuby ran on it too; C# plugs its own binder into it from the Microsoft.CSharp assembly.

cards.q: dynamic d = GetList(); int n = d.Count + 1; How many call sites does the compiler create for the second statement?
cards.explain: Three operations on dynamic: get the Count member (GetMember), add 1 (BinaryOperation) and convert the dynamic result to int (Convert). Each is its own call site with its own binder.

wrong.2: Do not forget the conversion: d.Count + 1 is dynamic too, and assigning it to an int needs a separate call site with a Convert binder.

cards.title: Three cache levels: L0, L1, L2
cards.body:
site.Target is the call itself. Inside is a compiled rule: a type check (restrictions) and an action. While the types match, a direct call runs with no reflection.

  • L0 is the Target delegate itself, built from the history of this site.
  • L1 is the array of recent rules of this call site, up to 10.
  • L2 is the binder shared rule cache, up to 128; sites with the same binder share it.

Only when all three levels miss does the binder analyze the call from scratch.
cards.deep:
The numbers come from the System.Linq.Expressions sources: CallSite.MaxRules = 10, RuleCache.MaxRules = 128. When L1 is full, old rules are evicted and the new one goes first. L2 belongs to a binder instance, and Microsoft.CSharp tries to reuse equivalent binder objects so that different sites share the cache.

The binder returns the rule as an expression tree, which the DLR compiles into a delegate. Where code generation is unavailable, expression trees run in an interpreter, which is much slower.

cards.q: An object of a new type reaches a call site for the first time. Put what happens in order
items: L0: the rule in site.Target does not match the type
L1: try the recent rules of this call site
L2: look in the binder shared cache
The binder analyzes the call using C# rules for the real types
The new rule is compiled into a delegate and stored in the caches
cards.explain: Each level costs more than the previous one. The binder is the most expensive step: it does the C# compiler work at run time, using reflection over the real types.

cards.title: What dynamic costs at each level
cards.body:
An L0 hit is a delegate call plus a type check. More than a direct call, but no reflection.

A new type at a call site means binding: semantic analysis by C# rules, building an expression tree, compiling it. That is orders of magnitude more than a call. The very first dynamic in a process also loads Microsoft.CSharp and warms up the binder itself.

A polymorphic site that receives dozens of types in turn keeps missing L0 and searching L1 and L2.

And wherever a value type travels as dynamic or comes back as the result of a dynamic operation, it is boxed.
cards.deep: Hence the recipe: if you need dynamic (COM, schemaless JSON), keep it at the edge and cast the result to a static type right away. If the types are known up front, use an ordinary interface or a generic method. If you need dispatch by member name over a limited set of types, a cached delegate from the previous lesson is usually faster and more predictable.

cards.q: Where does dynamic pay noticeably more than an ordinary call? Select all.
options: The first call at a site with a new argument type
A site that receives dozens of different types in turn
A repeated call with the same type when the rule is already in L0
A value type passed as dynamic
cards.explain: A new type means binding and compiling a rule. Many types mean L0 misses and cache searches. A value type in dynamic is boxed. An L0 hit is the cheapest path: a delegate and a type check.

cards.title: Source generators: reflection at compile time
cards.body:
Reflection at run time reads metadata to learn which properties and methods a type has. But all of that was already known to the compiler. A source generator does this work at build time.

A generator is a class from an analyzer assembly that Roslyn loads right into the compiler process. It sees the syntax trees and the semantic model, the same type information that reflection would later read from metadata, and adds new C# files to the compilation. It cannot change existing code, so everything is built on partial.
cards.deep:
The modern API is IIncrementalGenerator (Roslyn 4.0, .NET 6 SDK): the generator describes a pipeline, and Roslyn caches intermediate results. That matters because generators also run in the IDE on every code change. The old ISourceGenerator reran from scratch and is considered obsolete.

You can see the generated code in the IDE under the project analyzers node, or write it to disk with the EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles property.

cards.q: Match the .NET generator with what it replaces
pairs: Inspecting types with reflection on first serialization
A P/Invoke marshalling IL stub built at run time
Boxing arguments and parsing the template when logging

cards.title: What you gain and where the limit is
cards.body:
The gains:

  • startup: no walking types with reflection and no IL generation at launch;
  • trimming and Native AOT: ordinary code is visible to analysis, the trimmer will not cut members that are needed, and no code generation is required at run time;
  • errors at build time, not in production; the generated code can be read and debugged.

The limit: a generator sees only what exists at compile time. Types from plugins loaded at run time will still need reflection.
cards.deep: A link back to the first lesson. Native AOT has no JIT: the compiler builds canonical code for reference T and a separate copy for every value T it managed to see. typeof(List<>).MakeGenericType(typeof(Point)) with a struct that appears nowhere else has nothing to run on at run time: there is no code, and nobody to create it. The analyzer warns about this (IL3050, RequiresDynamicCode). With a reference argument such a call usually works: the shared List<__Canon> code fits.

cards.q: The app is published with Native AOT. Why may typeof(List<>).MakeGenericType(typeof(Point)) fail for a struct Point that is not used in generics anywhere else?
options: No JIT: machine code for List<Point> was not compiled ahead of time
Native AOT does not support generics
MakeGenericType is forbidden in Native AOT for any arguments
A struct cannot be a List<T> argument under AOT
cards.explain: Every value T needs its own copy of the code. The AOT compiler builds only the copies it sees in the program. For a reference argument the shared List<__Canon> code would do.

wrong.2: With reference arguments MakeGenericType usually works: the shared canonical code is already compiled.

cards.q: Declare a regex that the generator builds at compile time
cards.explain: You write the declaration of a partial method, the generator writes its body: C# code that matches the string the way RegexOptions.Compiled would, but with no Reflection.Emit at run time. The [GeneratedRegex] attribute arrived in .NET 7.

cards.q: Where does source generator code run?
options: Inside the compiler during the build and in the IDE
In the runtime the first time the type is used
In the JIT when a method is compiled
After compilation, by rewriting the IL of the finished assembly
cards.explain: A generator is part of compilation: Roslyn loads it into its own process and adds its output to the sources. The finished assembly contains ordinary compiled code; the generator itself does not end up in it.

wrong.3: That is how IL rewriting tools (IL weaving) work. A generator runs earlier and emits C# source code, not IL.

lessons.title: Final: generics and reflection inside out
lessons.sub: __Canon, dictionaries, tokens, Invoke, call sites and generators

cards.q: The method Echo<T>(T x) is called with int, double, string and Uri. How many machine code versions will the JIT produce (ignoring tiered recompilation)?
cards.explain: Echo<int> and Echo<double> get a copy each, while string and Uri share the canonical Echo<__Canon>. Three in total.

wrong.1: string and Uri are reference types, so both use the same code: Echo<__Canon>.

cards.q: Which line prints False?
cards.explain: Cache<string> and Cache<object> run shared code, but each has its own statics block and its own static constructor. So their Guids differ. Two reads of Cache<string>.Id give the same value.

cards.q: T is a reference type and the code is shared (__Canon). Which operations inside the method need a generic dictionary lookup? Select all.
options: new List<T>()
o is T
return default(T);
typeof(T)
if (x == null)
cards.explain: Creating a List<T>, checking a type and getting a Type all require the exact T. default(T) for a reference T is just null, and a null check does not depend on the type.

cards.q: Version 2 of a library changed void Log(string s) into void Log(string s, int level = 0). The old app was not rebuilt. What happens on Log("hi")?
options: MissingMethodException: the app MemberRef has a one-parameter signature
It works: level becomes 0
A warning at startup, then the call goes through
The runtime picks the nearest overload by name
cards.explain: A MemberRef token stores the name and the full signature. The new assembly has no Log(string), and the default value is inserted by the compiler of the calling code, which the old app never saw.

wrong.1: The value 0 would have been inserted by the compiler when building the app. The app was built against the old version, and its IL calls a one-parameter method.

cards.q: Order the ways to call a method from fastest to slowest (in general, for a method with int parameters)
items: A direct call
A delegate from CreateDelegate
MethodInvoker.Invoke (.NET 8)
MethodInfo.Invoke with a cached MethodInfo
GetMethod by name and Invoke on every call
cards.explain: A direct call can be inlined. A delegate is an indirect call without checks. MethodInvoker saves the array but boxes the arguments. Invoke also allocates the array. A lookup by name each time adds reflection cache work on top.

cards.q: Match each part of dynamic with its role
pairs: The rule inside the site.Target delegate
Up to 10 recent rules of this call site
Analyzes the call by C# rules at run time
An object in a hidden static field per operation

cards.q: What is true about source generators and Native AOT? Select all.
options: A generator only adds code; it cannot change existing code
The JSON generator removes reflection-based type inspection at startup
In Native AOT, MakeGenericType with a struct not seen at compile time may fail
A generator runs the first time a method is called
cards.explain: A generator runs inside the compiler and only adds files, which is why it relies on partial. Without a JIT there is nobody to create a code copy for a new value T.

cards.q: Reach the private field _count without reflection (.NET 8)
cards.explain: For a static extern method marked [UnsafeAccessor], the runtime substitutes direct field access at JIT time: no MethodInfo, no boxing, and it works in Native AOT.

units.title: Runtime performance
units.blurb: How .NET makes code fast on the fly: JIT tiers, OSR and Dynamic PGO, ReadyToRun versus Native AOT, inlining and devirtualization — and how to measure the result honestly with BenchmarkDotNet. Course final.

lessons.title: JIT tiers and Dynamic PGO
lessons.sub: Tier 0, Tier 1, OSR and a live profile

cards.title: The JIT dilemma: compile fast or run fast
cards.body:
In the unit "How .NET code runs" you saw two passes: Tier 0, then Tier 1. Now for the why.

An optimizing JIT is expensive: inlining, register allocation and removing array bounds checks all cost compile time. Yet at startup thousands of methods run once or twice: static constructors, reading configuration, registering services. Optimizing them is wasted time.

So Tier 0 is built with almost no optimizations: no inlining, locals live on the stack rather than in registers. The code is worse, but it is ready fast. Code is made good only where it pays off — in hot methods.
cards.deep:
In .NET Framework and early .NET Core the JIT always compiled with full optimizations, and NGen took care of fast startup. Tiered compilation arrived in .NET Core 2.1 as an opt-in and has been on by default since .NET Core 3.0.

Tier 0 is essentially the same minopts mode the JIT uses for Debug builds. You can turn tiers off entirely with <TieredCompilation>false</TieredCompilation>: every method is then compiled optimized right away, startup gets slower, and Dynamic PGO disappears.

cards.title: How a method becomes hot
cards.body:
Tier 0 code sits behind a call counter. Once a method reaches the threshold — about 30 calls — it is queued. A background thread compiles an optimized version, and when it is ready the method entry point is redirected to the new code.

The program does not stop: threads already inside the old code finish there, and new calls go to the new code.

Counting does not start right away. While the JIT is busy compiling new Tier 0 methods at startup, counting is postponed: otherwise all the initialization code would end up "hot".
cards.deep:
Runtime knobs for experiments: DOTNET_TC_CallCountThreshold (the threshold, 30 by default) and DOTNET_TC_CallCountingDelayMs (the counting delay, 100 ms by default; it is extended while new Tier 0 methods keep appearing). These are internal settings, not a public contract: the values can change between versions.

Tier 1 is the end of the line. If the program behaves differently later, the method is not recompiled again.

cards.task: A service handles requests. Call HandleRequest ("×10" speeds things up) until Parse reaches Tier 1. Then call LoadConfig once — where does it stay?

cards.q: LoadConfig was called once at startup. What code will it have until the process ends?
options: Tier 0: it will never reach the threshold
Tier 1: the background thread eventually optimizes everything
Tier 1 after the first garbage collection
None: the code is unloaded after the call
cards.explain: Recompilation is triggered only by the counter. A cold method stays in Tier 0 — and rightly so: there is no point optimizing code that will not run again.

wrong.1: The background thread only takes methods from the hot queue, and they get there through the call counter.

cards.title: A long loop: OSR
cards.body:
The problem: Main is called once, and inside is a loop of a billion iterations. The call counter never reaches 30, so the loop would spin in slow Tier 0.

Before .NET 7 the JIT dodged this crudely: a method with a loop was compiled optimized straight away, skipping Tier 0, and startup paid for it.

Since .NET 7 on x64 and Arm64 there is OSR (on-stack replacement). Tier 0 loop code contains patchpoints with an iteration counter. When the counter fires, the JIT builds an optimized version of the method that can start mid-loop, moves the current values of the locals into it, and execution continues there.
cards.deep:
The OSR version is a special variant of the method: it is entered only from a patchpoint, and its frame sits on top of the Tier 0 frame. The next ordinary call goes the usual way through the counter. JIT output marks such a version as OSR.

The behavior for methods with loops is controlled by <TieredCompilationQuickJitForLoops>: true (the default since .NET 7 where OSR exists) means Tier 0 first, false means optimized code straight away, as before.

cards.q: Main is called once, and inside is a loop of a billion iterations. How does .NET 8 on x64 make this loop fast?
options: OSR: it switches to an optimized version of the method mid-loop
It does not: Main never reaches 30 calls and stays in Tier 0
It compiles Main optimized right away because it has a loop
It restarts Main from the beginning, now in Tier 1
cards.explain: The counter sits on loop iterations, not only on calls. When it fires, the JIT builds the OSR version and continues from the current iteration, keeping the values of i and sum.

wrong.1: That is what would happen without OSR. This is exactly the gap OSR closes.
wrong.2: That is what the JIT did before .NET 7. Now a method with a loop also starts in Tier 0.
wrong.3: A restart would repeat the side effects of the code before the loop. OSR continues from the same spot.

cards.title: Dynamic PGO: a profile from the live program
cards.body:
PGO (profile-guided optimization) means the compiler looks at how the code actually behaves. Dynamic PGO collects the profile right inside the running process:

  • which if branches run and which almost never do;
  • which concrete types arrive at virtual and interface calls;
  • which methods sit behind delegates.

Tier 1 is compiled with this data: the hot path goes straight, cold blocks move to the end of the method, and the common type is called directly (more on that in lesson 3). Dynamic PGO appeared in .NET 6 as an opt-in and has been on by default since .NET 8.
cards.deep:
In .NET 8 profile counters are not placed in the first Tier 0: that would slow down all startup code. A hot method goes Tier 0 → instrumented Tier 0 → Tier 1, roughly 30 calls per step. Code from a ReadyToRun image takes another route: R2R → optimized instrumented Tier 1 → Tier 1. Methods with loops that are eligible for OSR skip plain Tier 0 and start instrumented right away.

The profile lives in process memory and is lost on restart. So the machine code of two runs can differ, depending on what input arrived during warmup.

cards.q: The life of a hot method in .NET 8 with default settings. Put the steps in order.
items: First call: the stub calls the JIT
Tier 0: quick code without optimizations
An instrumented version collects the profile
A background thread compiles Tier 1 using the profile
The entry point is redirected to the new code
cards.explain: Cheap and fast first, then the profile, and only then the expensive optimization. Switching to the new code happens without stopping the program.

cards.title: static readonly becomes a constant
cards.body:
Tier 1 has an advantage no ahead-of-time compiler has: by the time of recompilation the class static constructor has already run. The JIT reads the value of a static readonly field and substitutes it as a constant.

If s_trace is false, the logging branch disappears entirely in Tier 1 — no check, no call. Tier 0 cannot do this: it is built before the value is known for sure.
cards.deep:
This works for references too: if a static readonly field holds an object, the JIT knows its exact type and can call its methods directly. With an ordinary (non-readonly) static field the trick does not work — the value may change.

Native AOT cannot know the value of an environment variable at build time. It can run simple static constructors ahead of time, during compilation, but anything that depends on the environment stays a runtime check.

cards.q: What does Tier 1 do that Tier 0 does not? Select all.
options: Inlines small methods
Uses values of static readonly fields as constants
Takes the Dynamic PGO profile into account
Compiles the method on its first call
Keeps all locals on the stack
cards.explain: Compiling on the first call is exactly what Tier 0 does. Tier 0 also keeps locals on the stack: allocating registers for them is an optimization Tier 0 does not have.

cards.title: How to see the tiers for yourself
cards.body:
Since .NET 7 JIT output is available in the regular runtime, no checked build needed. Two environment variables:

  • DOTNET_JitDisasmSummary=1 — a list of all compilations: which method and at what tier (Tier 0, instrumented, Tier 1, OSR);
  • DOTNET_JitDisasm=Name — the machine code of every version of a method. You can see where a call was inlined and where a call remained.

DOTNET_JitStdOutFile redirects this output to a file. To compare "with PGO and without" there are the project properties TieredPGO, TieredCompilation and the environment variables DOTNET_TieredPGO=0, DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0.
cards.code:
# every compilation with its tier
DOTNET_JitDisasmSummary=1 dotnet run -c Release

# machine code of every version of Work
DOTNET_JitDisasm=Work dotnet run -c Release
cards.deep: Counters without a restart: dotnet-counters monitor -n MyApp shows the number of compiled methods and the time spent in the JIT. From inside the program, System.Runtime.JitInfo.GetCompiledMethodCount() and JitInfo.GetCompilationTime() (.NET 6+) give the same. In BenchmarkDotNet the [DisassemblyDiagnoser] attribute shows the machine code.

cards.q: Turn off Dynamic PGO in the project file to compare speed with and without it
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <___>false</___>
</PropertyGroup>
cards.explain: TieredPGO=false turns off only the profile; the tiers stay. TieredCompilation=false would remove the tiers and PGO along with them. Without rebuilding — the DOTNET_TieredPGO=0 variable.

cards.q: A hot method got [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.AggressiveOptimization)] so that it "is Tier 1 right away". What happens?
options: The method is optimized right away, but without a PGO profile — and may end up slower than regular Tier 1
The method gets faster under any conditions
Since .NET 8 the attribute is ignored
The method is compiled ahead of time, as in ReadyToRun
cards.explain: AggressiveOptimization takes the method out of the tiered scheme: full optimization on the first call, no instrumentation. No profile means no PGO gains, and static fields may not be initialized yet at compile time. Usually you do not need the attribute.

wrong.1: Optimization without a profile can be worse than Tier 1 with one. Check with a measurement.

lessons.title: ReadyToRun and Native AOT by the numbers
lessons.sub: Startup, size and peak speed

cards.title: Three ways to get machine code
cards.body:
You already know three routes: the regular JIT, ReadyToRun (precompiled code next to the CIL) and Native AOT (the whole program ahead of time, no JIT). Now let us compare them on three axes:

  • startup — how long until the first useful action;
  • size — on disk and in memory;
  • peak speed — how fast hot code runs after warmup.

The fourth axis is what stops working. There is no universal winner: each option buys something and pays for it with something else.

cards.title: What startup is made of
cards.body:
Startup of a regular app: the host finds the runtime, the CLR initializes, assemblies load — and the JIT compiles every method on its first call. A web service has thousands of such methods, and JIT time can be a noticeable share of startup.

The .NET libraries themselves ship in ReadyToRun format, so the JIT mostly gets your code and generic instantiations. Exactly how much — you can ask the runtime.
cards.deep: JitInfo exists since .NET 6. From outside, dotnet-counters monitor shows the same: counters for compiled methods, IL bytes and time in the JIT from the System.Runtime provider. Good practice is to measure startup with these numbers before and after turning on ReadyToRun rather than take it on faith.

cards.q: An ASP.NET Core service starts slowly, and a noticeable part of startup is the JIT. The code uses reflection heavily and loads plugins from a folder. What should you try first?
options: ReadyToRun: less JIT at startup and no restrictions
Native AOT: startup will be the fastest
Turn off tiered compilation
Put AggressiveOptimization on hot methods
cards.explain: ReadyToRun is compatible with everything regular .NET can do: if the precompiled code is not enough, the JIT steps in. Native AOT cannot load plugins from a folder.

wrong.1: Native AOT does not load assemblies on the fly, and reflection under it needs preparation. For this service it means a big rework.
wrong.2: Without tiers every method is compiled fully optimized right away — startup gets slower.
wrong.3: This attribute turns off tiers for the method: compilation is more expensive and there is no profile. It will not help startup.

cards.title: ReadyToRun: the catch
cards.body:
R2R code is built ahead of time by the crossgen2 compiler, but it has to survive updates of the runtime and neighboring assemblies. Hence the limits:

  • methods from other assemblies cannot always be inlined: they may change after publishing;
  • the code targets a common instruction set, not the one the machine actually has;
  • there is no Dynamic PGO profile at build time.

So R2R code counts as the initial tier: it replaces Tier 0, and the JIT still recompiles hot methods into Tier 1. Startup is faster, peak speed is the same as with the regular JIT. The price is size: the file holds both CIL and machine code.
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <RuntimeIdentifier>linux-x64</RuntimeIdentifier>
  <PublishReadyToRun>true</PublishReadyToRun>
</PropertyGroup>
cards.deep:
The boundary within which inlining is allowed is called the version bubble. Composite R2R (PublishReadyToRunComposite, usually together with self-contained) compiles the app and the framework as one piece: the boundary is wider and more inlining happens, but you can no longer update the runtime separately.

Then and now: NGen in .NET Framework built images for a specific machine and framework version and regenerated them after every update. An R2R image is portable: if the code does not fit, the runtime simply discards it and calls the JIT.

cards.q: Why is ReadyToRun code usually slower than Tier 1 on the hot path? Select all.
options: Methods from other assemblies are inlined with restrictions
The code targets a common instruction set, not this processor
There is no Dynamic PGO profile at build time
An R2R file contains no CIL
R2R code is run by an interpreter
cards.explain: That is exactly why hot R2R methods are recompiled into Tier 1. The file does contain CIL — without it recompilation would be impossible. There is no interpreter: R2R is ordinary machine code.

cards.title: Native AOT: the whole program ahead of time
cards.body:
The ILC compiler starts at Main, finds everything reachable, throws away the rest (trimming) and compiles to machine code. A small runtime goes alongside: the garbage collector, the type system, exception handling — no JIT. The result is a single executable for a single platform.

What it gives you:

  • startup — the fastest: no CIL to load, nothing to compile;
  • memory — less: no JIT, no JIT data structures, no Tier 0 code;
  • size — for a simple program on the order of a few megabytes, and .NET does not need to be installed.
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
  <OptimizationPreference>Speed</OptimizationPreference>
</PropertyGroup>
cards.deep:
OptimizationPreference takes Speed or Size: a trade-off between code speed and file size. Native AOT builds for a specific RID; cross-compiling between operating systems is not supported.

Native AOT sees the whole program at once (closed world). If a class has no subclasses, the compiler can treat it as effectively sealed and call its methods directly. The JIT has no such knowledge: a new assembly with a subclass may load at any moment.

cards.q: Match the project property to what it does
pairs: A single native file without a JIT
The runtime ships with the app

cards.title: Peak speed: who leads after warmup
cards.body:
Native AOT starts fastest of all, but over a long run the JIT has its own trump cards:

  • the JIT knows the real processor and uses its instructions: checks like Vector256.IsHardwareAccelerated are constants for it;
  • the JIT has the Dynamic PGO profile and the values of static readonly fields.

Native AOT is built by default for a conservative instruction set and without a profile, but it is optimized from the start and sees the whole program. The qualitative summary:

  • startup: Native AOT < ReadyToRun < JIT;
  • peak speed: JIT ≈ ReadyToRun after warmup, Native AOT close — sometimes a bit lower, sometimes higher.

The peak difference is usually small and depends on the code — only a measurement on your own workload decides.
cards.deep: The instruction set for Native AOT is raised with the IlcInstructionSet property — but then the file will not run on processors without those instructions. The answer to "which is faster" changes from version to version: both the JIT and ILC improve noticeably in every .NET release, so old comparisons from the internet go stale.

cards.q: A service runs for weeks without restarts under constant load. Only peak throughput matters. What will most likely give the best result (and is worth checking with a measurement)?
options: The regular JIT with tiers and Dynamic PGO
Native AOT
ReadyToRun with the JIT turned off
A Debug build with the JIT
cards.explain: Startup does not matter here, and over a long run the JIT adapts to the processor and the load profile. Native AOT may turn out no worse — but its wins are primarily startup and memory.

wrong.1: The strengths of Native AOT are startup, memory and not depending on an installed .NET. For peak speed over a long run the JIT has more data.
wrong.2: You cannot turn off the JIT for an R2R app: it is needed for hot methods and for everything missing from the image.
wrong.3: In Debug the JIT does not optimize at all.

cards.title: The price of Native AOT: what stops working
cards.body:
The Native AOT world is closed: everything that will run must be known at build time. Therefore:

  • you cannot load a new assembly (Assembly.LoadFrom) or generate code (Reflection.Emit);
  • reflection over members that nothing in the code references may not find them — trimming cut them out;
  • Expression.Compile() works through an interpreter — slower.

The compiler warns you in advance: IL2xxx — trimming problems, IL3xxx — AOT problems. The cure is source generators: code that used to be built by reflection at run time is written at build time.
cards.deep: A library only needs <IsAotCompatible>true</IsAotCompatible> (.NET 8+): the trimming and AOT analyzers turn on, and warnings show up in a normal build rather than at the consumer. There are generators for System.Text.Json, regular expressions ([GeneratedRegex]), logging ([LoggerMessage]) and configuration binding.

cards.q: What works under Native AOT without rework? Select all.
options: LINQ over in-memory collections
System.Text.Json with a JsonSerializerContext
Loading plugins with Assembly.LoadFrom
Generating code with Reflection.Emit
Regular expressions with [GeneratedRegex]
cards.explain: LINQ is ordinary code, and generators write code at build time. Loading assemblies and Emit require a JIT, and Native AOT has none.

cards.q: A simple console app was published four ways. Order them from the smallest output to the largest.
items: Framework-dependent .dll (the runtime is already on the machine)
Native AOT
Self-contained with trimming
Self-contained without trimming
cards.explain: Orders of magnitude: the .dll is kilobytes, but .NET must be installed; Native AOT is a few megabytes; self-contained with trimming is around ten megabytes; without trimming it is tens of megabytes, the whole runtime and libraries. Exact numbers depend on the version and the OS.

cards.q: Build Native AOT that puts code speed above file size
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <___>true</___>
  <OptimizationPreference>___</OptimizationPreference>
</PropertyGroup>
cards.explain: PublishAot turns on Native AOT, and OptimizationPreference=Speed asks ILC to prefer faster code even if the file ends up bigger.

lessons.title: Inlining, devirtualization and measuring
lessons.sub: Inlining, sealed, guarded devirtualization and BenchmarkDotNet

cards.title: Inlining: the call is gone
cards.body:
Inlining means the JIT copies the body of the called method straight into the caller. The savings on the call itself are modest. What matters is what opens up afterwards: the JIT sees the arguments and the body together and can simplify the code further — fold constants, drop array bounds checks, keep a struct in registers.

Recall from lesson 1: Tier 0 inlines nothing. Inlining is the job of Tier 1, R2R and Native AOT.
cards.deep:
The decision is made from the callee CIL. A rough picture of the RyuJIT heuristics: very small methods (around 16 bytes of IL — getters, wrappers) are inlined almost always; larger ones go through a benefit model that weighs constant arguments, loops and the profile; methods above roughly 100 bytes of IL are usually not inlined. The thresholds are an implementation detail and change between versions.

The price of inlining is larger machine code. Too much inlining bloats hot code and hurts the instruction cache, which is why the JIT is careful.

cards.q: Why does inlining often speed code up by more than the call itself costs?
options: Once the body is inserted, the JIT sees the arguments and can simplify the code further
The inlined method runs in parallel on another core
The garbage collector does not run in inlined code
Inlined code is saved to disk and never recompiled
cards.explain: A call costs little. The win is in the optimizations that become possible once the method body and its arguments are in one place: constants fold, checks disappear.

cards.title: What blocks inlining
cards.body:
• Size: inlining a large body does not pay off.
  • Virtual calls: for a virtual or interface call the JIT does not know whose body to insert.
  • Exception handling: for a long time methods with try/catch/finally were never inlined; in .NET 10 the JIT learned to inline some of them, mainly those with try/finally.
  • throw: a method that only throws is not inlined, and a throw inside bloats the body.
  • Recursion and [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.NoInlining)].

[MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining)] lifts the size limit but not the others: a virtual call still will not be inlined with it. The classic trick is to move the throw into a separate method so the hot one stays small.
cards.deep:
The .NET libraries themselves work this way: internal ThrowHelper classes keep all the throwing code apart. The JIT sees that the method does not return and moves its call into the cold part of the code.

The runtime reports why inlining did not happen through the MethodJitInliningFailed event with a text reason (visible in PerfView and dotnet-trace). Quicker is to look at the machine code via DOTNET_JitDisasm: if a call remains, it was not inlined.

cards.q: Get is tiny, yet it will not be inlined into Sum. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: Get is virtual: this may be a subclass of Cache with a different Get, and the JIT does not know whose body to insert. Making the class sealed or dropping virtual helps.

cards.title: Devirtualization: getting a direct call back
cards.body:
If the JIT has proven the exact type of the object, a virtual call becomes a direct one — and it can be inlined. Where the JIT learns this from:

  • the class or method is sealed — there can be no subclasses with another body;
  • the object was created right there with new;
  • the object sits in a static readonly field and Tier 1 sees its type (lesson 1);
  • it is a struct: nothing derives from it.

So sealed on classes without subclasses is a free hint to the JIT. Analyzer CA1852 suggests sealing internal classes that have no subclasses.
cards.deep:
Generics over structs: for every value type T the JIT makes a separate copy of the code, so in M<T>(T x) where T : IShape the call x.Area() on a struct becomes direct and gets inlined. For reference T the code is shared and the type is unknown there (more in the unit on generics inside out).

sealed speeds up type checks too: obj is Circle for a sealed class is a single type pointer comparison, no hierarchy walk.

cards.title: Guarded devirtualization: betting on the profile
cards.body:
Often the type is statically unknown: anything can arrive in Any(Shape s). But Dynamic PGO sees that in practice it is almost always Circle. Then Tier 1 performs guarded devirtualization (GDV): it checks the type with a single comparison and on the common path calls the method directly — with inlining.

The fallback is an ordinary virtual call, so the code is correct for any type. If the load changes, the check simply starts missing more often: Tier 1 is not rebuilt. The same trick works for interface calls and delegates.

cards.q: When can the JIT call s.Area() directly or inline it? Select all.
options: Circle is sealed and the variable has type Circle
The object was just created with new Circle() in the same method
The PGO profile showed that Circle almost always arrives (with a type check)
Area is marked AggressiveInlining and the object type is unknown
The method runs in Tier 0
cards.explain: The exact type is required: from sealed, from a nearby new, or from the profile — under a check. AggressiveInlining does not say whose body to insert, and Tier 0 does not inline at all.

cards.title: BenchmarkDotNet: a measurement you can trust
cards.body:
Why a Stopwatch around a single call lies: the first call includes the JIT and slow Tier 0, a Debug build is unoptimized, a single run drowns in noise, and a garbage collection caused by other code can land in the middle of the measurement.

BenchmarkDotNet does all this for you: it builds the project in Release, runs each benchmark in a separate process, warms the method up until timings are stable, does many iterations and computes statistics. It will refuse to run an unoptimized build.
cards.deep:
Run it with dotnet run -c Release. Columns: Mean — the average, Error — half of the 99.9% confidence interval, StdDev — the spread, Ratio — relative to the Baseline, Allocated and Gen0 — from [MemoryDiagnoser].

You can compare runtimes and settings in one run: [SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.Net80)], [SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.NativeAot80)], and through the job configuration — environment variables such as DOTNET_TieredPGO=0. [DisassemblyDiagnoser] shows the machine code that was actually measured.

cards.q: In the benchmark above, Sealed got a Ratio of about 0.97 — nearly the same as Virtual. Why is the difference so small?
options: Dynamic PGO did guarded devirtualization: Virtual also has Circle.Area inlined behind a type check
BenchmarkDotNet cannot measure virtual calls
A virtual call in .NET costs nothing
The measurement ran in a Debug build
cards.explain: _any always holds a Circle, the profile saw it, and Tier 1 put in a type check with the inlined body. What remains is the cost of one comparison. Set DOTNET_TieredPGO=0 and the gap will most likely grow.

wrong.2: By itself a virtual call is an indirect jump and a barrier to inlining. Here PGO hid it.
wrong.3: BenchmarkDotNet will not run in Debug — it checks that the build is optimized.

cards.title: Fooling yourself: dead code and laziness
cards.body:
• Dead code elimination: if the result is unused, the JIT may throw the computation away, and you measure nothing. Return the result from the method: BenchmarkDotNet will "consume" it.
  • Constant folding: Square(5) becomes 25 at compile time. Keep inputs in fields, set them with [Params] and prepare them in [GlobalSetup].
  • LINQ laziness: return an IEnumerable and you only measured creating the query. Enumerate the sequence: .Consume(consumer) with BenchmarkDotNet Consumer.

cards.q: Which benchmark measures almost no work?
cards.explain: Where is lazy: Filter only creates the query object, and filtering never starts. BenchmarkDotNet consumes the returned reference but will not enumerate it. Count and ToArray walk the whole array.

cards.q: Match the BenchmarkDotNet attribute or class to its purpose
pairs: Ratio column relative to the reference
Enumerate a sequence so it is not thrown away
Machine code of the measured method

cards.q: How does BenchmarkDotNet run a single benchmark? Put the steps in order.
items: Builds a separate project in Release
Starts a separate process
Picks the number of calls per iteration (pilot)
Warms the method up until timings are stable
Runs the main measurements and computes statistics
cards.explain: A separate process cuts off the influence of other code and another JIT state. The pilot picks the call count so an iteration is not too short for the timer. Warmup brings the method to Tier 1, and only then do the measurements run.

lessons.title: Course final: .NET inside out
lessons.sub: From CIL to the hot path — test yourself

cards.q: The path of a hot method from source to the best machine code in .NET 8
items: The C# compiler turns the method into CIL
CIL and metadata go into the assembly
First call: the stub calls the JIT and Tier 0 comes out
An instrumented version collects the profile
A background thread builds Tier 1 using the profile
cards.explain: The whole course in one chain: the compiler, the assembly, the JIT on demand, and then the runtime refines hot code from a live profile.

cards.q: A command-line tool runs thousands of times a day in CI and works for a fraction of a second. No reflection, no plugins. What gives the biggest win?
options: Native AOT: no JIT and no CIL loading at startup
Dynamic PGO: the profile will speed up hot methods
AggressiveOptimization on every method
Turn off tiered compilation
cards.explain: The program lives so briefly that almost nothing reaches Tier 1: all the time is startup. Native AOT removes the JIT entirely, and its restrictions do not get in the way here.

wrong.1: PGO pays off over long runs. In a fraction of a second the profile has no time to be collected, let alone used.
wrong.3: Without tiers every method is compiled fully optimized right away — startup only gets slower.

cards.q: What is true about code after warmup? Select all.
options: A static readonly bool can become a constant in Tier 1, and the branch disappears
AggressiveInlining lets you inline a virtual call with an unknown type
sealed helps the JIT call a method directly
Tier 0 inlines small methods
Guarded devirtualization keeps a fallback virtual call
cards.explain: AggressiveInlining only lifts the size limit: it cannot tell whose body to insert when the type is unknown. Tier 0 inlines nothing.

cards.q: Which line allocates a heap object for a boxed int?
cards.explain: Assigning a value type to object is boxing: an object with a header and a type pointer appears on the heap. Unboxing with (int)o copies the value back, and int to long is an ordinary widening with no heap involved.

cards.q: Match the course concept to what it means
A method was timed with a Stopwatch: one call right after the program started. What was actually measured?
options: JIT time and slow Tier 0 code, not the steady-state speed
The peak speed of the method after warmup
Only garbage collection time
The speed of code from a ReadyToRun image
cards.explain: The first call goes through the stub and the JIT, and the resulting code is Tier 0 without inlining. Only warmup and many iterations show the steady-state speed — which is what BenchmarkDotNet does.

cards.q: Add an allocations column and a comparison against the reference
cards.explain: [MemoryDiagnoser] adds Allocated and Gen0, Baseline = true adds a Ratio column relative to Old. Both methods return their result, so the JIT will not throw the computation away.

cards.q: What is missing from an app built with Native AOT? Select all.
options: A JIT at run time
Tiered compilation and Dynamic PGO
A garbage collector
Loading new assemblies on the fly
Type information for GetType()
cards.explain: The garbage collector and the type system are part of the small Native AOT runtime — memory is still managed and GetType works. There is no JIT, and so no tiers, no PGO and no loading of new code.

cards.q: A program uses List<int>, List<long>, List<string> and List<object>. How many distinct machine-code versions of the Add method will the JIT produce?
cards.explain: Every value type T gets its own copy: int and long. All reference T share one piece of code — a reference is always pointer-sized. Three in total.

wrong.1: string and object are reference types; they share code.
wrong.2: int and long differ in size and the code handles them differently — the copies are separate.
